url: /vlo/api/host/functions/remoteReporter.md
---
[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [host](../index.md) / remoteReporter

# Function: remoteReporter()

> **remoteReporter**(`completeUrl`, `token`, `fetchImpl?`): [`TaskReporter`](../interfaces/TaskReporter.md)

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/reporters.ts:30](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/reporters.ts#L30)

Reports over HTTP to the host that owns the task. `completeUrl` is the task's base URL
(`…/v1/tasks/{id}`); the three verbs hang off it. Each call has a 10 s timeout and throws
a plain `Error` on a non-2xx answer, which for `heartbeat` is how a lost lease surfaces.

## Parameters

### completeUrl

`string`

### token

`string` | `undefined`

### fetchImpl?

[`FetchLike`](../type-aliases/FetchLike.md) = `globalThis.fetch`

## Returns

[`TaskReporter`](../interfaces/TaskReporter.md)

---

---
url: /vlo/api/host/functions/runPullWorker.md
---
[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [host](../index.md) / runPullWorker

# Function: runPullWorker()

> **runPullWorker**(`options`): `Promise`<`void`>

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/pull.ts:71](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/pull.ts#L71)

Runs until `signal` aborts, then resolves once the tasks in flight have reported. Throws
a `TypeError` when there is no queue to poll. A failed poll goes to `onError` and the loop
retries after 1 s. Runs on the worker side; the host only needs the `api` role.

## Parameters

### options

[`PullWorkerOptions`](../interfaces/PullWorkerOptions.md)

## Returns

`Promise`<`void`>

## Example

```ts
import { defineWorker, runPullWorker } from "@oona/vlo/host";

const abort = new AbortController();
const loop = runPullWorker({
  baseUrl: "https://vlo.example.com",
  token: "control-plane-token",
  worker: defineWorker(
    { "pull.render": (input: { clip: string }) => ({ rendered: input.clip.toUpperCase() }) },
    { queues: ["media"] },
  ),
  waitMs: 5_000,
  signal: abort.signal,
  onError: (error) => console.error(error),
});
process.once("SIGTERM", () => abort.abort());
await loop;
```

url: /vlo/api/host/functions/serve.md
---
[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [host](../index.md) / serve

# Function: serve()

> **serve**(`options`): `Promise`<[`ServeResult`](../interfaces/ServeResult.md)>

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/roles.ts:305](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/roles.ts#L305)

Binds a port, tells the host its own URL, then starts it. `publicUrl` is set to the
listener's URL unless the options give one, so pushed tasks carry a working `complete_url`.

## Parameters

### options

[`ServeOptions`](../interfaces/ServeOptions.md)

## Returns

`Promise`<[`ServeResult`](../interfaces/ServeResult.md)>

## Example

```ts
import { serve } from "@oona/vlo/host";

const server = await serve({
  journal: "postgres://user:pass@localhost/app",
  workflows: [pipeline],
  activities: [render],
  auth: { token: "control-plane-token" },
  port: 4100,
});
console.log(server.url); // http://127.0.0.1:4100
await server.close();
```

# Function: signalRun()

> **signalRun**(`ctx`, `runId`, `name`, `payload`): `Promise`<[`SignalRunResult`](../interfaces/SignalRunResult.md)>

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/runs.ts:116](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/runs.ts#L116)

Stores a signal and, when the run is waiting on that name, delivers it in the same
transaction. Validated against the registered signal schema when there is one. Never
answers 409 for an ended run: the signal is stored and reported as not delivered.

## Parameters

### ctx

[`HostContext`](../interfaces/HostContext.md)

### runId

`string`

### name

`string`

### payload

[`Json`](../../index/type-aliases/Json.md)

## Returns

`Promise`<[`SignalRunResult`](../interfaces/SignalRunResult.md)>

## Throws

[BadRequest](../classes/BadRequest.md) when the payload fails the schema.

## Throws

[RunNotFound](../classes/RunNotFound.md) when no run has that id.

# Function: signPush()

> **signPush**(`secret`, `taskId`, `attempt`, `tsMs`, `body`): `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/signature.ts:32](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/signature.ts#L32)

Signs a push: `v1=` + HMAC-SHA256 over `taskId.attempt.tsMs.sha256(body)`, hex. The
dispatcher's HTTP transport calls this; a custom transport signs the same way.

url: /vlo/api/host/functions/signSignalLink.md
---
[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [host](../index.md) / signSignalLink

# Function: signSignalLink()

> **signSignalLink**(`secret`, `link`): `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/links.ts:53](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/links.ts#L53)

Mints the token for a link: `v1.<expiresAtMs>.<hmac-sha256 hex>`. The host's
`POST /v1/runs/{id}/links/{name}` route does this for you; call it directly to mint
links out of band with the same secret ([linkSecret](linkSecret.md)).

## Parameters

### secret

`string`

### link

[`SignalLinkClaims`](../interfaces/SignalLinkClaims.md)

## Returns

`string`

## Example

```ts
const token = signSignalLink(secret, {
  runId: "run_1",
  name: "approve",
  expiresAtMs: Date.now() + DEFAULT_LINK_TTL_MS,
});
verifySignalLink(secret, token, "run_1", "approve", Date.now()); // true
```

# Function: verifySignalLink()

> **verifySignalLink**(`secret`, `token`, `runId`, `name`, `nowMs`): `boolean`

[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [host](../index.md) / verifySignature

# Function: verifySignature()

> **verifySignature**(`secret`, `headers`, `rawBody`, `nowMs?`): `boolean`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/signature.ts:53](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/host/worker/signature.ts#L53)

True when the `vlo-*` headers sign `rawBody` with `secret` and the timestamp is within
5 minutes of `nowMs` (default `Date.now()`). Missing or malformed headers are false, never
thrown; the comparison is timing-safe.

### secret

`string`

### headers

[`HeaderSource`](../interfaces/HeaderSource.md)

### rawBody

`string`

### nowMs?

`number` = `...`

## Returns

`boolean`

# Interface: AgentLoopOptions

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/loop.ts:44](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/loop.ts#L44)

Tools that wait for a person's yes before they run. A rejected call becomes an
observation and the decider chooses again. See [ApprovalOptions](ApprovalOptions.md).

# Interface: ApprovalOptions

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:30](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L30)

What `agentLoop({ approval })` takes.

## Properties

### name?

> `optional` **name?**: `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:34](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L34)

Signal name prefix. Default [DEFAULT_APPROVAL_SIGNAL](../variables/DEFAULT_APPROVAL_SIGNAL.md).

***

### onTimeout?

> `optional` **onTimeout?**: `"fail"` | `"reject"`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:41](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L41)

What an unanswered request becomes: `"reject"` (default) tells the decider the call was
not approved and carries on; `"fail"` fails the run.

***

### timeoutMs?

> `optional` **timeoutMs?**: `number`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:36](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L36)

How long to wait for a reply. Without one the run waits until somebody answers.

***

### tools

> **tools**: readonly `string`\[]

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:32](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L32)

Names of the tools that need a yes before they run. Each must be a key of `tools`.

[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [agent](../index.md) / DecisionOptions

# Interface: DecisionOptions\<I>

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:14](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L14)

`@oona/vlo/agent` — the agent layer, built on the authoring surface of `@oona/vlo`.

An agent is the reducer model in its purest form: state is memory plus budget, the event
is an observation, the command is the next tool call. Nothing here does I/O; `agentLoop`
returns a `WorkflowDef` you hand to `defineWorkflow`.

## Type Parameters

### I

`I` *extends* `z.ZodType`

## Properties

### input

> **input**: `I`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:16](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L16)

What the decider is shown. `agentLoop` sends `{ goal, memory, candidate, score }`.

***

### queue?

> `optional` **queue?**: `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:20](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L20)

***

### retry?

> `optional` **retry?**: [`RetryOptions`](../../index/interfaces/RetryOptions.md)

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:19](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L19)

***

### timeoutMs?

> `optional` **timeoutMs?**: `number`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:22](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L22)

Wall-clock ceiling for one decision; the host fails the task with `cause: "timeout"`.

***

### tools

> **tools**: `Record`<`string`, [`Activity`](../../index/interfaces/Activity.md)>

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts:18](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/decision.ts#L18)

The tools it may pick from, keyed by the name it returns in `tool`.

# Interface: ToolApproval

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:20](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L20)

The reply to an approval request. An empty payload approves, so a signed link's
confirmation form is enough; `approved: false` rejects.

## Properties

### approved?

> `optional` **approved?**: `boolean`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:22](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L22)

`false` rejects the call. Absent or `true` approves it.

***

### by?

> `optional` **by?**: `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:26](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L26)

Who replied.

***

### reason?

> `optional` **reason?**: `string`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts:24](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/agent/approval.ts#L24)

Why, shown to the decider when the call is rejected.

# Type Alias: AgentPhase

> **AgentPhase** = `"decide"` | `"approval"` | `"tool"` | `"evaluate"` | `"parked"` | `"done"`

# Function: fakeClock()

> **fakeClock**(`startMs`): [`Clock`](../interfaces/Clock.md)

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/journal/fixtures.ts:37](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/journal/fixtures.ts#L37)

A [Clock](../interfaces/Clock.md) that starts at `startMs` and only moves when `advance` is called, so
leases, timers and timeouts expire exactly when a test says so.

## Parameters

### startMs

`number`

## Returns

[`Clock`](../interfaces/Clock.md)

## Example

```ts
import { fakeClock } from "@oona/vlo/testing";

const clock = fakeClock(1_700_000_000_000);
const host = createHost({
  journal: "sqlite://:memory:",
  workflows: [workflow],
  now: clock.now,
  dispatcher: { tickMs: 10 },
});
await host.start();
clock.advance(60_001); // one whole default lease and a millisecond
```

[@oona/vlo](../../packages.md) / [testing](../index.md) / journalConformance

# Function: journalConformance()

> **journalConformance**(`name`, `open`): `void`

Defined in: [sdk/ts/sdk/src/journal/conformance.ts:38](https://github.com/oonalab/vlo/blob/a81c115e42e129b4efe8fd86066744a4f8bc3670/sdk/ts/sdk/src/journal/conformance.ts#L38)

Registers the journal conformance suite as a vitest `describe` block named `name`.

`open` is called before every case and must return a fresh, empty journal; the suite
runs `migrate()` on it and `close()`s it afterwards. The cases check the durability
promises the host relies on: gap-free `seq` under concurrent transactions, all-or-nothing
transitions, stale-attempt and terminal-task rejection, lease and timeout reaping,
once-only timers, schema upserts, signal buffering, run queries and idempotent migration.
Call it from a test file, not from application code.

## Parameters

### name

`string`

### open

() => `Promise`<[`Journal`](../../host/interfaces/Journal.md)>

## Returns

`void`

## Example

```ts
import { openJournal } from "@oona/vlo/host";
import { journalConformance } from "@oona/vlo/testing";

let index = 0;
journalConformance("sqlite journal", async () =>
  openJournal(`sqlite://./.vlo/conformance-${++index}.db`),
);
```

# Why Vlo

Vlo is durable execution that is tiny, performant, reliable, efficient and built to run at
the edge. This page explains what each of those buys you, why one design principle makes
all five possible, and what Vlo does not have yet.

## What durable execution costs today

Durable execution keeps long-running work alive through crashes. It usually makes you pay
five costs that have nothing to do with your product.

| Cost | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Heavy** | The engine is a server cluster, a large server binary or a hosted state store, and often a message broker as well. |
| **Slower as runs grow** | Engines that resume by re-running the workflow from the top do more work on each resume as a run's history grows. |
| **Fragile resumes** | That re-run must behave identically every time. One clock read or random number in the wrong place breaks recovery, and you find out in production. |
| **Tied to one place** | A platform engine runs on one cloud. A server engine needs machines in a region you operate. Either way the engine decides where your work lives. |
| **Costly while idle** | A cluster runs whether or not there is work, and waiting workflows often hold a worker or a slot. |

## The five benefits

### Tiny

Vlo is small enough to be a library in your app instead of a system beside it.

* **298 KB kernel.** Rust compiled to wasm, 297,573 bytes. With the Node host it is under
  600 KB. CI fails the build if the kernel passes 1 MiB or the runtime JavaScript passes
  256 KB. See [limits.md](./limits.md#size-budgets-ci-gate).
* **Nothing to stand up.** There is no server, no cluster and no broker. You add a package
  and point it at a database.
* **A closed model.** Five event kinds, seven commands and seven statuses. That is the
  whole programming model, and projects cannot extend the kernel.
* **A small surface for you, too.** One config file, four CLI verbs, three adapters, and a
  hello-world in three files.

### Performant

Vlo's speed comes from doing little work per step, and the amount of work does not grow
with the run.

* **One transaction per step.** The event, the new state and the next tasks commit
  together. There is no second system to coordinate with.
* **Constant-cost resume.** State is rewritten with every event, so waking a run is: load
  one row, verify its hash, continue. A run with 20,018 events resumed in the same time as
  a run with 38.
* **No broker hop.** A task is a row committed with the event. A worker in the same process
  skips HTTP entirely, and a polling worker is woken the moment a task is written.
* **Small rows.** Payloads over 256 KiB move to a content-addressed blob store, so the
  journal stays light.

The measured numbers, their setup and their limits are in [performance.md](./performance.md).

### Reliable

A crash at any point loses nothing, and wrong state cannot pass unnoticed.

* **Commit before acknowledge.** Nothing is confirmed to a caller or a worker until it is
  in the journal.
* **A transactional outbox.** Tasks, timers and child runs are rows written with the event.
  A crash between "saved" and "sent" is picked up on the next pass by any node.
* **Leases and heartbeats.** A worker that dies stops heartbeating, the lease lapses, and
  the retry policy decides what happens next.
* **State that checks itself.** Every checkpoint carries a hash that is verified on every
  load. A run rebuilt from its journal is compared step by step, and a mismatch fails the
  run at the exact event.
* **Recovery never depends on re-running your code.** Vlo resumes from stored state.
  Reducers must still be pure, but a mistake shows up as a failed rebuild, not as a
  silently different run.

The full list of guarantees, and what each one does not promise, is in
[reliability.md](./reliability.md).

### Efficient

Vlo uses resources only while a step is actually running.

* **Waiting is free.** Between events a run holds no compute, no open connection and no
  suspended stack. A run waiting two days for an approval is about 2 KB of rows.
* **Workers scale to zero.** Tasks are pushed over HTTP, so workers can be serverless
  functions that exist only while they work.
* **No infrastructure tax.** The journal is the Postgres you already run, and it is also
  the queue.
* **One process to start.** Orchestrator, API and workers are roles of a single process.
  You split them only when load calls for it.
* **Efficient with model spend.** The kernel meters tokens and cost on every event,
  including failed attempts. An agent that reaches its budget parks until someone tops it
  up. See [agents.md](./agents.md).
* **Efficient with your time.** One command for local development on a SQLite file, with no
  Docker and no cloud account, and generated deploy files for Cloud Run and Vercel.

### Built for the edge

Vlo is designed so the engine goes to the data, instead of the data going to the engine's
cluster.

* **A kernel with no I/O.** It only decides. It returns a write-set of rows and the host
  writes them, so it runs anywhere wasm runs: a container, a serverless function, a laptop.
* **A run lives where its journal lives.** One journal and one writer per run gives total
  order with no consensus protocol.
* **One durability model.** Commit before acknowledge, everywhere. The edge is a place to
  deploy, never a weaker tier.

**Status: the edge host is not built yet.** Today Vlo runs on Node: Cloud Run, Vercel, a
container or a laptop. A Cloudflare host with a Durable Object journal is the next platform
milestone. Nothing in the kernel needs to change to get there, but until it ships, do not
plan on running Vlo in an edge runtime. See [status.md](./status.md).

## One design principle

A Vlo workflow is one pure function:

```
(state, event) → (state, commands)
```

1. Something happens to a run: it started, a task finished, a signal arrived, a timer
   fired, or a child run ended. That is an event.
2. The kernel appends the event to the run's journal and hands it to your reducer with the
   current state.
3. The reducer returns the new state and a list of commands: run a task, set a timer, start
   a child run, wait for a signal, emit, complete, or continue as a new run.
4. The event, the new state and the commands are saved in one database transaction.
5. The host carries the commands out, pushing tasks to workers and firing timers.

The five benefits are one chain of consequences from that function:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R["A workflow is a pure reducer, so it never suspends"]
  R --> E["Nothing is held between events → efficient"]
  E --> T["No stack capture, sandbox or replay driver → tiny"]
  T --> G["A tiny kernel with no I/O runs anywhere wasm runs → built for the edge"]
  R --> P["State is rewritten with every event, so a resume is one read → performant"]
  R --> L["A pure function can be hashed and re-checked, one transaction per step → reliable"]
```

Three phrases carry the idea:

* **State is the snapshot.** There is exactly one checkpoint per run, rewritten with every
  event. Recovery loads it, checks its hash and carries on.
* **The journal is the queue.** A task is a row committed in the same transaction as the
  event that asked for it.
* **Nothing suspends.** No function is ever paused mid-line, so there is no stack to save
  and no code to re-run.

## How this differs from other designs

Every durable engine must answer one question: when the process dies halfway, how does the
work continue? There are four answers.

| Model | How progress survives a crash | What it asks of you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Replayed code** | The workflow function runs again from the top. Recorded step results are replayed, so it fast-forwards to where it stopped. | Deterministic workflow code. Replay work grows with history. Mistakes are caught after the fact. |
| **State-machine definition** | The workflow is data, not code. The service stores the current state. | Logic in JSON or YAML. Branches and loops are verbose. |
| **Snapshotted runtime** | The whole runtime instance is checkpointed and resumed. | A server that owns the runtime, and large snapshots. |
| **Event-sourced reducer** (Vlo) | Each event is folded into a state snapshot inside one transaction. There is nothing to replay. | Workflows written as pure reducers, or with the `sequence` helper. No `await` inside a workflow. |

The first three keep the same assumption: a workflow is a running program that must be
paused and brought back. They differ in how they bring it back. Vlo drops the assumption.
A workflow is never running, so it never needs to be paused, saved or resumed. It is only
ever asked one question: given this state and this event, what next?

## The trade

You give up writing a workflow as straight `await a(); await b();` code. In exchange,
recovery never depends on re-running that code.

The `sequence` helper covers linear pipelines, so most workflows read as a list of steps:

```ts
sequence([step(plan), fanOut(work, selectItems, { concurrency: 2 }), waitFor(approve), step(finish)]);
```

An agent loop is one call to `agentLoop`. Reducers are plain functions, so you unit test
them with no engine running. See [workflows.md](./workflows.md) and [testing.md](./testing.md).

## What Vlo does not have yet

Check this list before choosing it.

* **No console.** There is no web UI with a run tree. Vlo has the journal, a live event
  stream, the HTTP API and the CLI. See [observability.md](./observability.md).
* **Workflows are TypeScript only.** Workers can be written in any language; the reducer
  runs in the Node host.
* **No managed cloud.** You run the host. `vlo deploy` renders the Cloud Run or Vercel
  files, but nobody operates it for you.
* **No edge host.** The Cloudflare host and Durable Object journal are planned, not built.
* **Nothing enforces reducer purity.** A TypeScript reducer is a plain function, so it
  could read the clock or call the network, and no lint catches that today. A mistake
  surfaces only when a run is rebuilt from its journal.
* **Benchmarks are local only.** One laptop, with the database on the same machine. There
  is no production or large-scale figure yet.
* **Known weak spots.** A step makes about 15 database round trips, so the host must sit
  beside its journal. One run that fans out very wide slows down sharply; wide work belongs
  in child runs. See [limits.md](./limits.md#known-weak-spots).
* **It is young.** Older engines have years of production history that Vlo does not.

## When to pick it

Pick Vlo when:

* you want durable workflows and agents without operating a server;
* your Postgres is already the system of record you trust;
* workers live in more than one language or more than one place;
* idle cost matters, because your runs spend most of their life waiting;
* you want agents with budgets that park instead of fail.

Pick a different engine when your team writes long linear workflows and wants them to read
as plain `await` code, or when you need a console and a support contract on day one.

Next: [getting-started.md](./getting-started.md), or the common objections in
[faq.md](./faq.md).

---
# Performance

Vlo does little work per step, and that work does not grow with the run. This page gives
the measured numbers, the setup they came from, and what they do not show.

**The headline result: resume time is flat.** A run with 20,018 events resumes as fast as a
run with 38.

## Why it is fast

* **One transaction per step.** The event, the new state and the next tasks commit
  together.
* **State is the snapshot.** One checkpoint per run is rewritten with every event, so a
  resume loads one row and checks one hash, however long the run is.
* **The journal is the queue.** A task is a row committed with the event. There is no
  broker hop, and a worker in the same process skips HTTP entirely.
* **Small rows.** Payloads over 256 KiB move to a content-addressed blob store.

## Setup

Read every number on this page together with this setup.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Machine | Apple M2 laptop, 8 cores |
| Runtime | Node 24.6 |
| Date | 27 November 2026 |
| Journal | On the same machine in both columns: a SQLite file, and Postgres 14 over localhost |
| Workers | In-process |
| Resume figures | The median of 7 fresh processes each |

These are local engine numbers. There is no network between the host and the database, and
no replication. See [What these numbers are not](#what-these-numbers-are-not).

## Steps and workflows

| Measure | SQLite | Postgres 14 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One step, committed, median | 0.33 ms | 0.96 ms |
| One step, committed, p99 | 0.65 ms | 1.62 ms |
| Steps per second, in sequence | About 3,000 | About 1,000 |
| A 3-step workflow, start to finish, median / p99 | 3.1 ms / 3.9 ms | 7.6 ms / 11.1 ms |
| A 5-step workflow, start to finish, median / p99 | 4.7 ms / 5.9 ms | 11.7 ms / 12.8 ms |
| Tasks completed across 2,000 separate runs, per second | 975 | 721 |
| Host start: load the kernel and open the journal | 2.3 ms | 9.0 ms |

## Resume

A resume here is a cold process loading a run and continuing it.

| Run length | SQLite | Postgres 14 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 38 events | 7.7 ms | 10.5 ms |
| 2,018 events | 7.9 ms | 10.6 ms |
| 20,018 events | 7.7 ms | 10.7 ms |
| Worst case: full rebuild from the journal, 20,018 events | 464 ms | 468 ms |

The worst case is a rare path. It runs only when a checkpoint is missing or was written by a
different workflow build, and it costs about 23 microseconds per event. See
[reliability.md](./reliability.md#state-that-checks-itself).

## Footprint and idle cost

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Kernel file size | 297,573 bytes |
| Kernel load time | 2.1 ms |
| Memory the kernel adds to a process | About 400 KB |
| Storage for one parked run | About 1.3 KB on SQLite, 2.0 KB on Postgres |
| Processes needed while 5,000 runs wait | 0 |

Ten thousand waiting runs are about 20 MB of rows on Postgres and no compute.

## What these numbers are not

* **They are not production numbers.** No figure here was measured with a network between
  the host and its database.
* **Step time follows the database round trip.** One step is about 15 database round trips,
  so step time is roughly 15 times the round trip. Against a remote Postgres with a 23 ms
  round trip, a step took 336 ms and a resume about 400 ms. Resume stayed flat there too:
  398 ms for a run with 30 events and 400 ms for one with 410. **Keep the host in the same
  region as its journal.**
* **Throughput is not a ceiling or a scale test.** The 721 tasks per second came from one
  laptop and one client starting runs in sequence. Vlo has not been load-tested on server
  hardware.
* **One very wide run is slow.** 1,000 tasks inside a single run finished at 45 per second,
  against 975 per second across separate runs. Per-task cost grows with the width of the
  run. This is a defect to fix; until then, put wide work in child runs with `fanOutRuns`.
  See [limits.md](./limits.md#known-weak-spots).
* **They are not a comparison.** Nothing here was measured against another engine on the
  same hardware, so these numbers do not show that Vlo is faster than anything else.

## How to read them

| Measure | Verdict | How to think about it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resume time as a run grows | Excellent | The line is flat. This is the result the design exists to produce. |
| Footprint | Excellent | Small enough that starting a process costs nothing noticeable. |
| Cost of waiting | Excellent | About 2 KB per parked run and no process. |
| One step | Good | About the cost of one small database transaction. Measured with no network, so it is a floor. |
| Small workflow, end to end | Good, with a caveat | Single-digit milliseconds on local Postgres, in an easy setup. |
| Worst-case rebuild | Acceptable | A rare path, about half a second for 20,018 events. |
| Throughput | Unproven | One laptop, one client. Not a scale test. |
| Database round trips per step | Weak | About 15. The largest lever on real-world speed. |
| Very wide fan-out in one run | Poor | A defect. Child runs avoid it today. |

## Practical guidance

1. Run the host in the same region as its journal, ideally the same network.
2. Use Postgres for anything beyond one process. SQLite is single-writer; see
   [limits.md](./limits.md#sqlite-is-single-writer).
3. Fan out wide work as child runs, not as hundreds of tasks in one run.
4. Keep state small, or compact long runs with `continue_as_new`. State over 256 KiB is
   read from the blob store on every event.

---
url: /vlo/reliability.md
---
# Reliability

Vlo is built so that a crash at any point loses nothing and wrong state cannot pass
unnoticed. This page states what Vlo guarantees, how each guarantee works, and what it
leaves to you.

## The guarantees at a glance

| Guarantee | In one line |
| --- | --- |
| [Commit before acknowledge](#commit-before-acknowledge) | Nothing is confirmed to a caller or a worker until it is in the journal. |
| [One transaction per step](#one-transaction-per-step) | The event, the new state and the next tasks are saved together or not at all. |
| [Nothing lost between "saved" and "sent"](#the-outbox) | Tasks, timers and child runs are rows; any orchestrator picks them up. |
| [Exactly-once recording](#exactly-once-recording-at-least-once-execution) | The first result recorded for an attempt wins. Execution is at-least-once. |
| [Dead workers are noticed](#leases-heartbeats-and-retries) | A lease that stops being renewed is reaped, and the retry policy takes over. |
| [State that checks itself](#state-that-checks-itself) | Every checkpoint is hash-checked on load. A rebuilt run is compared step by step. |
| [Typed, signed boundaries](#typed-and-signed-boundaries) | Inputs, outputs and signals are schema-checked. Pushed tasks are signed. |

## Commit before acknowledge

This is the one durability rule, and it is the same on every platform. A request to start a
run, deliver a signal or complete a task is answered only after its transaction has
committed. If the process dies before the answer, the caller retries and the journal
decides: the work is either recorded or it is not.

## One transaction per step

Every durable change goes through one path: lock the run, load the checkpoint, fold the
event, commit. The transaction holds the event, the new checkpoint and every row the
commands produced (tasks, timers, signal waits, child runs). There is no second system to
keep in step, because the journal is also the queue. See
[architecture.md](./architecture.md#the-write-path).

## The outbox

Commands are not executed inside the transaction. They are rows, and the dispatcher turns
rows into effects on its next pass: it starts runs, pushes tasks, fires timers, reaps
lapsed leases and tells parents about closed children.

* A crash between "committed" and "pushed" loses nothing. The row is still there, and the
  next pass on any process holding the `orchestrator` role picks it up.
* Every stage claims its rows, so several orchestrators can share one Postgres journal
  without doing the same work twice.
* Timers fire exactly once: the fired flag and the timer event commit together.

## Exactly-once recording, at-least-once execution

This is the honest guarantee a distributed system can make.

* Each attempt has an idempotency key, `run_id:step_id:attempt`.
* The first terminal result for an attempt wins. A later one is answered as a duplicate and
  changes nothing.
* A handler may still run twice for one key, for example after a crash. **Make a handler
  idempotent on `ctx.taskId` and `ctx.attempt` when its side effect matters.** See
  [activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#idempotency).

Vlo does not claim exactly-once execution.

## Leases, heartbeats and retries

* A task is held by a lease, not by a broker deadline. The SDK worker heartbeats
  automatically, so a task can run for hours.
* A worker that dies stops heartbeating. The lease lapses, the reaper fails the attempt
  with `heartbeat_lost`, and the retry policy decides what happens next.
* Retries use backoff with jitter. The default policy is 3 attempts, exponential, starting
  at 1 second.
* `schema_violation`, `user_cancel` and `nondeterminism_detected` are never retried.

Only a task's final outcome reaches your reducer. Retries happen below it.

## State that checks itself

Every checkpoint carries a hash, and the host verifies it every time it loads one.

If a checkpoint is missing, or was written by a different workflow build, the host rebuilds
the run from its first event and compares each step's hash with the one recorded in the
journal. A mismatch fails the run with `nondeterminism_detected` at the exact event,
instead of continuing with wrong state.

What this means for your code:

* **Normal recovery never re-runs your workflow.** It loads stored state and continues.
* **Reducers must be pure**: no clock, no randomness, no I/O. Time and entropy arrive on the
  event as `ts_ms` and `random`. See [workflows.md](./workflows.md#determinism).
* **Nothing enforces purity yet.** No lint or sandbox stops a reducer from reading the
  clock. An impure reducer is caught only when a run is rebuilt, and it is caught as a
  failed run, not as silently different state.

## Typed and signed boundaries

* Activity inputs are validated when a reducer asks for a task; outputs are validated
  before a result is folded. Registered signals are validated on arrival.
* Every pushed task carries an HMAC signature bound to the task, the attempt and the time,
  and is refused outside a five-minute window. A queue URL alone cannot be fed forged or
  replayed work.
* A signed link authorises one signal on one run until it expires. Opening the link
  changes nothing; it must be confirmed. See
  [signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md#signed-links).

## How the kernel is tested

The kernel is a pure library, which makes it the easiest part to test hard:

* property tests over the whole event pipeline;
* an exhaustive table of step transitions;
* golden fixtures in `fixtures/kernel/`, which any host in any language can replay;
* a CI gate that requires both the committed wasm and a freshly built one to pass every
  fixture.

Journal adapters share one conformance suite, `journalConformance` from
`@oona/vlo/testing`. See [kernel-protocol.md](./kernel-protocol.md).

## What you are responsible for

| Your part | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Keep reducers pure | Nothing enforces it yet. |
| Make side-effecting handlers idempotent | Execution is at-least-once. |
| Run the journal on durable storage | Vlo is as durable as the database under it. Back it up as you would any system of record. |
| Set `auth.token` on any reachable host | The control plane is plain HTTP behind a bearer token. |
| On serverless, run the cron tick | A manual dispatcher only advances when something calls it. See [deployment.md](./deployment.md#serverless-manual-dispatch). |

## See it

Kill the host while a run is waiting, restart it, and the run carries on. The walkthrough
is in [getting-started.md](./getting-started.md#kill-it-and-watch-it-continue).

# Status and roadmap

What is built, what is planned, and what is not on the list. Nothing on this page is a date
or a promise; planned items are listed in the order they are expected.

## Where Vlo runs today

| Target | Status |
| --- | --- |
| A laptop or CI, on a SQLite file | Built |
| Any Node host or container, on Postgres | Built |
| Google Cloud Run | Built, with generated deploy files |
| Vercel (serverless, with a cron tick) | Built, with generated deploy files |
| Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects) | **Not built.** Planned as the next platform milestone |
| AWS (Lambda or ECS, Aurora, S3, EventBridge) | Planned, after Cloudflare |

Vlo needs Node 22.5 or later today.

## What is built

| Piece | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Kernel as a wasm module with no I/O and no imports | 298 KB, capped at 1 MiB in CI |
| Write-set contract between kernel and storage | The kernel decides, the host persists |
| Postgres and SQLite journals | Postgres works behind transaction-mode poolers |
| Several orchestrators sharing one journal | On Postgres |
| Roles split across services | Push and pull workers anywhere, in any language |
| Serverless mode | A time-boxed drain plus a cron tick |
| Workflows | Hand-written reducers, `sequence`, `fanOut`, `fanOutRuns`, `waitFor`, `sleep`, child runs, `continue_as_new` |
| Signals and signed links | Human approvals, webhooks, deadlines |
| Agents | `@oona/vlo/agent`: decide, tool, evaluate, with budgets that park and tool calls that wait for approval |
| Usage accounting | Tokens, cost and CPU time banked in the kernel on every event |
| CLI | `vlo dev`, `vlo serve`, `vlo doctor`, `vlo deploy` |
| Blob stores | Local files and Google Cloud Storage |

## What is planned

| Piece | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Cloudflare: host in Workers, Durable Object journal, R2 blobs, alarm timers | Planned, the next platform milestone |
| Cross-run index on the edge | Planned; two designs recorded, not decided |
| Conformance test kit for third-party adapters | Planned |
| Native Rust host with no Node | Planned; `crates/traits` sketches the adapter traits |
| AWS adapters | Planned, after Cloudflare |
| Rust workflows as WASM components, Go and Python SDKs | Planned, later |
| A console: run tree, inbox, event timeline | Not built; see [observability.md](./observability.md#not-built-yet) |
| OpenTelemetry export | Not built |
| S3 and Vercel Blob stores | Not built |
| A lint for reducer purity | Not built |

## About "built for the edge"

The edge is the direction of the design, not a feature you can use today.

What is true now:

* The kernel compiles to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with no imports, which is the form an
  edge runtime needs.
* The kernel returns a declarative write-set, so any storage that can apply one atomic
  write can be a journal.
* Every run has one journal and one writer, which is the shape of a Durable Object.

What is not true yet:

* There is no Durable Object journal adapter and no Workers host.
* The host opens its journal with `pg` or `node:sqlite`, both of which need Node.

So the accurate statement is: Vlo is built to run at the edge, and it does not run there
yet. See [limits.md](./limits.md#not-available-on-edge-runtimes-yet).

## Known weak spots

These are measured and documented, and they are work to do:

* About 15 database round trips per step, so the host must sit beside its journal.
* One run that fans out very wide slows down sharply. Use child runs.
* No benchmark at scale or over a network.

Details are in [performance.md](./performance.md#what-these-numbers-are-not) and
[limits.md](./limits.md#known-weak-spots).

## Stability

Vlo is young. The kernel protocol is versioned and gated by golden fixtures, and the
changelog records every release: see
[`../CHANGELOG.md`](../CHANGELOG.md). Pin a version and read the changelog before you
upgrade.

---

---
url: /vlo/faq.md
---
# FAQ

Quick answers and common objections. For the full argument see [why-vlo.md](./why-vlo.md).

## Choosing Vlo

### What is Vlo, in one sentence?

An open-source durable execution engine for workflows and AI agents that runs as a library
on your own Postgres or a SQLite file.

### What do I need to run it?

Node 22.5 or later and a database: Postgres for production, a SQLite file for a laptop, CI
or a small single-process host. There is no server, broker or cluster to install.

### I want to write plain `await` code. Can I?

No, and that is the one real trade. A Vlo workflow is a reducer, not a function that
pauses. The `sequence` helper makes pipelines read as a list of steps, and `agentLoop`
builds an agent in one call. If straight `await a(); await b();` code matters most to your
team, a replay-based engine is the better fit.

### Reducers sound hard. Are they?

The hello-world workflow is about ten lines. Most workflows are a `sequence` and never
touch a reducer directly. When you do write one, it is a plain function you can unit test
with no engine running. See [testing.md](./testing.md).

### Is it production-ready?

It is young, and it says so. The kernel is small enough to audit, tested with property
tests and golden fixtures, and every checkpoint is hash-checked on load. It has no
console, no managed cloud and no benchmark at scale. Read [status.md](./status.md) and
[limits.md](./limits.md) before you commit to it.

### Is there a UI?

Not yet. The journal is a table you can query, every run has a live event stream, and the
HTTP API and CLI cover the rest. See [observability.md](./observability.md).

### What about lock-in?

Vlo is Apache-2.0. The state is rows in your database, on your cloud. Nothing is hosted for
you.

### Does it run on the edge?

Not yet. The kernel is built for it: a wasm module with no I/O. The host and journals need
Node today, and the Cloudflare host is the next platform milestone. See
[status.md](./status.md#about-built-for-the-edge).

## Performance and scale

### How fast is it?

On a laptop with local Postgres, a 3-step workflow finishes in under 8 ms and a resume
takes about 10 ms whether the run has 38 events or 20,000. Those are local numbers with no
network. See [performance.md](./performance.md) for the setup and the caveats.

### Is my database fast enough to be the queue?

For most products, yes: the design is bounded by the database, in the low thousands of
tasks per second on Postgres. If you already run a broker, it can carry tasks as a delivery
transport, and the journal still records everything.

### Where should the host run?

In the same region as its journal. One step makes about 15 database round trips, so a slow
link to the database makes every step slow.

### Can one run fan out to thousands of tasks?

Use child runs for that. One run with very many tasks slows down sharply; `fanOutRuns`
gives each item its own run and avoids the problem. See [limits.md](./limits.md#known-weak-spots).

### How much does a waiting run cost?

About 2 KB of rows on Postgres and no compute. A run waiting two days for an approval
holds no process, no connection and no stack.

## Building

### Can I write workflows in Python or Go?

Not yet. Workflows are TypeScript. Workers can be written in any language that can serve
or call HTTP. See [recipes.md](./recipes.md#write-a-worker-in-another-language).

### Which model providers does the agent layer support?

All of them, because it calls none of them. Your worker makes the model call and reports
what it spent. See [agent-harness.md](./agent-harness.md).

### What happens when an agent runs out of budget?

The run parks. Its status becomes `awaiting_signal`, it keeps its memory and its best
result, and it resumes when someone sends a top-up. It does not fail and it does not keep
spending. See [agents.md](./agents.md#parking-and-top-ups).

### Can an agent ask a person before it does something risky?

Yes. Name the tools that need approval in `agentLoop({ approval })`. When the model picks
one, the run waits without holding compute until someone approves or rejects it, by API
call or by a signed link. A rejection goes back to the model as an observation. See
[agents.md](./agents.md#approving-tool-calls).

### How long can a task run?

As long as it needs. A task is held by a lease that the worker renews, so there is no
broker deadline. Set `timeoutMs` only if you want a ceiling.

### Will my handler ever run twice?

It can. Execution is at-least-once and recording is exactly-once. Make a handler idempotent
on `ctx.taskId` and `ctx.attempt` when its side effect matters. See
[reliability.md](./reliability.md#exactly-once-recording-at-least-once-execution).

### Can I change a workflow while runs are in flight?

Carefully. A run pins the workflow's name, not its code. If you change a reducer's logic
and a live run is later rebuilt from its journal, the rebuild no longer matches and the run
fails with `nondeterminism_detected`. Let in-flight runs finish, or register the changed
workflow under a new name. See [workflows.md](./workflows.md#determinism).

### What must a reducer not do?

Read the clock, generate randomness, or do I/O. Time and entropy arrive on the event as
`ts_ms` and `random`; everything else belongs in an activity. Nothing enforces this yet, so
treat it as a rule of the road.

### How do I test a workflow?

Call `workflow.reduce` directly for unit tests, or start an in-process host on a throwaway
SQLite journal for end-to-end tests. See [testing.md](./testing.md).

## Operating

### Does it work on serverless?

Yes. The host runs with a manual dispatcher: the request that starts or signals a run
drains it, and a cron tick is the backstop. `vlo deploy` renders the files for Vercel and
Cloud Run. See [deployment.md](./deployment.md#serverless-manual-dispatch).

### Does it work behind a connection pooler?

Yes, including transaction-mode poolers. The Postgres journal keeps no session state. See
[journal.md](./journal.md#postgres-adapter).

### How do I see what a run did?

`GET /v1/runs/{id}/events` or `client.events(runId)` returns the journal: every step,
attempt, retry, cause, error and usage figure. See [observability.md](./observability.md).

### A run failed with `nondeterminism_detected`. What now?

Treat it as a bug report. A reducer no longer reproduces the history it wrote, usually
because it read a clock or random value, or its logic changed under a live run. The error
names the event where it diverged. See [errors.md](./errors.md).

### Something is misconfigured. Where do I start?

`vlo doctor --profile <name>`. It runs real round trips against the journal, the blob
store, the kernel and each queue, and prints a hint for anything that fails. See
[cli.md](./cli.md).

---

---
url: /vlo/getting-started.md
---
# Getting started

In ten minutes you will have a durable workflow running on your laptop, with no Docker and
no cloud account. Then you will kill the process and watch the run continue.

Vlo keeps long-running work alive through crashes and restarts. You write a workflow as a
pure reducer, `(state, event) → [state, commands]`, and Vlo saves each step in one database
transaction. Between steps a run is only rows in a database, so there is nothing to lose
when a process dies.

Building an agent? Do this page first, then go to [agent-harness.md](./agent-harness.md).

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @oona/vlo zod
```

* Node ≥ 22.5 (the SQLite journal uses `node:sqlite`).
* Zod 4 is a peer dependency. `@google-cloud/storage` is optional and only needed for a
  `gcs://` blob store.
* The `vlo` CLI ships with `@oona/vlo` (`npx vlo …`).

## The smallest program

Two files in one directory. The config says where the code and the journal live; the
workflow module exports a reducer.

```ts
// vlo.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineConfig({
  workflows: ["*.workflow.ts"],
  profiles: {
    local: { journal: "sqlite://.vlo/dev.db", blob: "file://.vlo/blobs" },
  },
});
```

```ts
// hello.workflow.ts
import { cmd, defineWorkflow } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineWorkflow("hello", {
  init: (input: { name: string }) => ({ greeting: `hello, ${input.name}` }),
  on: {
    started: (state) => [state, [cmd.complete(state.greeting)]],
    task_done: (state) => [state, []],
  },
});
```

`init` builds the initial state from the run input. `started` is the first event every run
receives; here it completes the run at once. `task_done` is required by the type even when
the workflow never schedules a task.

Relative imports inside the config and the modules it points at need explicit file
extensions (`./activities.ts`); the files are imported by Node, not bundled.

## Run it

```sh
npx vlo dev
  ✓ journal  sqlite:///home/me/app/.vlo/dev.db
  ✓ found 1 workflow   hello
  ✓ api      http://localhost:4100
```

`vlo dev` uses the `local` profile (or the only profile in the file), migrates the journal, loads every module the globs
match and serves the HTTP API on port 4100. A warning about "no workers found" is expected
here: this workflow has no activities. See [cli.md](./cli.md) for every flag.

## Start a run

With `curl`:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4100/v1/runs \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workflow":"hello","input":{"name":"world"}}'
# {"run_id":"run_…"}

curl -s http://localhost:4100/v1/runs/run_…
# {"run_id":"run_…","workflow":"hello","status":"completed","output":"hello, world",…}
```

With the client (it lives in `@oona/vlo/host`):

```ts
import { createClient } from "@oona/vlo/host";

const client = createClient({ baseUrl: "http://localhost:4100" });

const started = await client.start("hello", { name: "world" });
const done = await client.waitFor(started.run_id, "completed");
console.log(done.output); // "hello, world"

// Or follow the journal live over SSE until the run ends.
for await (const message of client.stream(started.run_id)) {
  if (message.type === "journal") console.log(message.seq, message.data.step_id);
  if (message.type === "end") console.log(message.data.status);
}
```

`client.get(runId)` returns the same run view as `GET /v1/runs/{id}`. The full route list
is in [http-api.md](./http-api.md).

## Add an activity and a worker

Real workflows do their non-deterministic work in activities, run by workers. The
`sequence` helper compiles a list of phases into a reducer.

```ts
// activities.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { activity } from "@oona/vlo";

export const shout = activity("hello.shout", {
  input: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ upper: z.string() }),
});
```

```ts
// shout.workflow.ts
import { defineWorkflow, sequence, step } from "@oona/vlo";
import { shout } from "./activities.ts";

export default defineWorkflow("shout", sequence([step(shout)]));
```

```ts
// shout.worker.ts
import { defineWorker } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineWorker({
  "hello.shout": (input: { text: string }) => ({ upper: input.text.toUpperCase() }),
});
```

Add the worker glob to the config and restart `vlo dev`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  workflows: ["*.workflow.ts"],
  workers: ["*.worker.ts"],
  profiles: { local: { journal: "sqlite://.vlo/dev.db", blob: "file://.vlo/blobs" } },
});
```

```ts
const started = await client.start("shout", { text: "hi" });
const done = await client.waitFor(started.run_id, "completed");
// done.output === { "hello.shout": { upper: "HI" } }
```

The worker runs in the same process as the engine. Moving it to another machine is a
config change, not a code change: see [activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md).

## Kill it and watch it continue

This is the point of durable execution, and you can see it in a minute. The
[pipeline example](../examples/pipeline/) plans three items, processes them two at a time,
then waits for a person. Run it from a checkout of the repository:

```sh
pnpm install                                               # once, from the repository root
cd examples && pnpm dev:pipeline                           # API on :4100
```

In a second terminal, start a run and look at it:

```sh
curl -s -X POST localhost:4100/v1/runs -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workflow":"pipeline","input":{"n":3}}'            # → {"run_id":"run_…"}
curl -s localhost:4100/v1/runs/<run_id>                    # "status":"awaiting_signal"
```

The run is now waiting for an approval. **Stop the host with Ctrl-C.** No process is
running for this run; it is a few rows in `examples/pipeline/.vlo/pipeline.db`.

Start the host again and approve:

```sh
pnpm dev:pipeline
curl -s localhost:4100/v1/runs/<run_id>                    # still "awaiting_signal"
curl -s -X POST localhost:4100/v1/runs/<run_id>/signals/pipeline.approve \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"by":"you"}'   # → {"delivered":true}
curl -s localhost:4100/v1/runs/<run_id>                    # "status":"completed"
```

The run finished with the work it did before the restart. Read its history, event by event:

```sh
curl -s localhost:4100/v1/runs/<run_id>/events
```

What happened: on restart the host loaded the run's one checkpoint row, checked its hash and
carried on. It did not re-run your workflow. A task that was in flight when the process
died is handled the same way with one extra step: its lease lapses (60 seconds by default)
and the retry policy starts a fresh attempt. See [reliability.md](./reliability.md).

## Examples

* [`../examples/hello/`](../examples/hello/) — the program above.
* [`../examples/pipeline/`](../examples/pipeline/) — plan → fan out → wait for a human → finish.
* [`../examples/agent/`](../examples/agent/) — an `@oona/vlo/agent` loop with a budget.
* [`../examples/harness/`](../examples/harness/) — an agent harness with a model worker and a tool that waits for approval.

---

# Concepts

One model underlies everything: a run is a journal of events, a workflow is a pure function
that folds those events into state and asks for effects, and the host executes the effects.

## Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Run** | One execution of a workflow. Has a `run_id`, a status, an ordered journal of events (`seq` 1, 2, 3…), and exactly one state checkpoint. |
| **Workflow** | A named reducer built with `defineWorkflow(name, { init, on })`. `init(input)` builds the first state; `on.<event>(state, event)` returns `[state, commands]`. |
| **Event** | Something that happened to a run: `started`, `task_done`, `signal`, `timer`, `child_done`. Every event carries `ts_ms`, 32 hex chars of journaled `random`, and the run's banked `usage_total`. |
| **Command** | What a reducer asks for: `task`, `timer`, `spawn`, `await_signal`, `emit`, `complete`, `continue_as_new`. Built with `cmd.*`; plain JSON. |
| **Step** | One unit of scheduled work inside a run, opened by a command: a task, a timer, a signal wait, a child run, or a marker. Identified by a `step_id` (`task#3`, or one you choose). |
| **Activity** | The declaration of a piece of non-deterministic work: a name, Zod input and output schemas, a retry policy, a queue. Content-hashed: `name@hash` is its `schema_ref`. |
| **Task** | A row in the journal that a worker executes to perform an activity. Has a `task_id` (`run:step`), an `attempt`, an `idempotency_key` (`run:step:attempt`), a lease and a retry policy. |
| **Signal** | A durable message into a run: a human reply, a webhook, a budget top-up. Declared with `signal(name, schema)`; delivered by `POST /v1/runs/{id}/signals/{name}`. Buffered if nothing is waiting yet. |
| **Timer** | A durable deadline. `cmd.timer({ ms })` parks the run; the host fires it as a `timer` event, exactly once. |
| **Child run** | A run started by `cmd.spawn`. When it ends, its parent receives `child_done` with the child's status and output. |
| **Journal** | Your Postgres database or a SQLite file. Holds runs, events, the state checkpoint, tasks, timers, signals. It is also the queue: there is no broker. |
| **Blob store** | A directory (`file://`) or a bucket (`gcs://`) for payloads over 256 KiB. The journal stores a `blob://sha256/<hex>` reference instead. |
| **Kernel** | The Rust state machine, compiled to wasm and loaded by the host. Validates events, calls your reducer, validates commands, and produces the write-set the journal applies. No I/O. |
| **Host** | The Node process around the kernel: opens the journal, serves HTTP, runs the dispatcher, runs in-process workers. `@oona/vlo/host`. |
| **Role** | What one host process does: `orchestrator`, `api`, `worker:<queue>`. A process may hold any subset. |
| **Worker** | Activity implementations: `defineWorker({ "name": handler })` plus the queues it serves. In-process, pushed to over HTTP, or polling. |
| **Profile** | One named deployment configuration in `vlo.config.ts`: journal, blob, roles, queues, auth, dispatcher mode, deploy target. |

## The loop

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant H as Host (api + orchestrator)
  participant K as Kernel (wasm)
  participant J as Journal
  participant W as Worker
  C->>H: POST /v1/runs
  H->>J: run row, status created
  H->>K: started event + init input
  K->>K: reducer(state, event) → [state, commands]
  K-->>H: write-set (events, tasks, timers…)
  H->>J: one transaction: event, checkpoint, task row
  H->>W: push task (HTTP or in-process)
  W-->>H: 202 accepted
  W->>H: POST /v1/tasks/{id}/complete
  H->>K: task_done event
  K-->>H: next write-set
  H->>J: commit
  H-->>C: SSE / GET /v1/runs/{id}
```

Every event goes through the same path: lock the run, load the checkpoint, fold, commit.
The dispatcher (the `orchestrator` role) reads committed rows on each tick and does the
effects: starts `created` runs, pushes `scheduled` tasks, fires due timers, reaps lapsed
leases and timeouts, and tells parents about closed children. A crash between "committed"
and "pushed" is recovered by the next tick, on any process holding the role.

## Statuses

Run status (`RunStatus`): `created` → `running` → `awaiting_signal` ⇄ `running` →
`completed` | `failed` | `cancelled` | `continued`. The last four are terminal; a run in a
terminal status accepts no further events.

Step status (`Status`): `scheduled`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `retrying`,
`cancelled`, `awaiting_signal`.

Failure cause (`Cause`): `timeout`, `heartbeat_lost`, `app_error`, `user_cancel`,
`schema_violation`, `nondeterminism_detected`. The last three are never retried.

## Roles

| Role | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `orchestrator` | The dispatcher: the only thing that turns rows into effects. Also the `POST /v1/timers/tick` route. |
| `api` | The control plane: `/v1/runs…`, `/v1/tasks/{id}/complete\|fail\|heartbeat`, `/v1/tasks/poll`. |
| `worker:<queue>` | Runs activities on `<queue>`: in-process when the orchestrator is the same process, or via `POST /v1/tasks/push` from a remote one. |

With no `roles` configured a process holds `orchestrator`, `api` and `worker:<q>` for every
queue its workers declare. Splitting is a profile change; see [deployment.md](./deployment.md).

## Two ways a task reaches a worker

* **Push** (default). The dispatcher POSTs the task to the queue's URL with an HMAC
  signature; the worker answers `202` and reports later on `complete_url`. A queue with
  no URL is served only by a worker in the same process.
* **Pull**. `mode: "pull"` queues are never pushed. Workers long-poll
  `POST /v1/tasks/poll` and get the same task shape.

Both share one accept path: the task is marked `running` with a lease in the same
transaction as the hand-off, so the reaper and crash recovery see no difference.

## Determinism, briefly

A reducer must be pure: no clock, no randomness, no I/O. Every non-deterministic input
(`ts_ms`, `random`, task outputs, signal payloads) arrives on the event. The host hashes the
checkpoint on every load and rebuilds it from seq 0 when it is missing; a rebuilt state that
disagrees with the journal fails the run with `nondeterminism_detected`. Details in
[workflows.md](./workflows.md#determinism).

## Further reading

* [why-vlo.md](./why-vlo.md) — what the reducer buys you, and what it costs.
* [reliability.md](./reliability.md) — what Vlo guarantees, in one place.
* [journal.md](./journal.md) — tables, dialects, the checkpoint.
* [kernel-protocol.md](./kernel-protocol.md) — the host ⇄ kernel calls.
* [architecture.md](./architecture.md) — how the pieces are laid out.

# Workflows

A workflow is a pure reducer. `defineWorkflow` gives it a name; the engine calls its
handlers with the current state and one event, and expects the next state and a list of
commands back.

```ts
import { cmd, defineWorkflow, type Reduction } from "@oona/vlo";
import { plan } from "./activities.ts";

interface State { stage: "planning" | "done"; n: number }

export default defineWorkflow("count", {
  init: (input: { n: number }): State => ({ stage: "planning", n: input.n }),
  on: {
    started: (state) => [state, [cmd.task(plan, { n: state.n })]],
    task_done: (state, event): Reduction<State> =>
      [{ ...state, stage: "done" }, [cmd.complete(event.output ?? null)]],
  },
});
```

## The contract

`defineWorkflow<S, I>(name, def)` takes:

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init` | `(input: I) => S` | Builds the state for the `started` event. `I` is whatever the run was started with. |
| `on.started` | `(state, event) => Reduction<S>` | Required. The first event of every run. |
| `on.task_done` | `(state, event) => Reduction<S>` | Required. A task attempt ended: `succeeded`, `failed` or `cancelled`. |
| `on.signal` | optional | A signal was delivered to an open wait. |
| `on.timer` | optional | A timer fired. |
| `on.child_done` | optional | A child run ended. |

`Reduction<S>` is `readonly [S, readonly Command[]]`. State must be JSON-serialisable: it is
stored as text, byte for byte, and handed back to the next handler with `JSON.parse`. No
classes, `Map`s or `Date`s.

An event with no handler throws, which fails the run. If you schedule a timer, implement
`on.timer`.

### Events

Every variant carries `type`, `ts_ms`, `random` (32 hex chars) and `usage_total`
(`{ cpu_ms, tokens, cost_micro_usd }`, the run's banked total including this event).

| Event | Extra fields |
| --- | --- |
| `started` | `input` |
| `task_done` | `step_id`, `attempt`, `activity`, `status`, `output?`, `cause?`, `error?`, `usage` (this attempt's own spend) |
| `signal` | `step_id`, `name`, `payload` |
| `timer` | `step_id` |
| `child_done` | `step_id`, `child_run_id`, `status`, `output?` |

Only a task attempt's *final* outcome reaches the reducer. Retries happen below it: a failed
attempt that the retry policy allows to try again is journaled as `retrying` and never
becomes a `task_done` event.

## Commands

Commands are plain objects. `cmd.*` builds them and validates what it can up front.

| Constructor | Command | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cmd.task(activity, input, { id?, queue? })` | `task` | Validates `input` against the activity's Zod schema and throws `ActivityInputError` if it does not match. Carries the activity's `schema_ref`, retry policy, lease and timeout. |
| `cmd.timer({ ms } \| { atMs }, id?)` | `timer` | Exactly one of `ms` (relative) or `atMs` (absolute epoch ms). |
| `cmd.spawn(workflow, input, { id? })` | `spawn` | `workflow` is a name or a `Workflow`. See [Child runs](#child-runs). |
| `cmd.awaitSignal(signal, { id?, timeoutMs? })` | `await_signal` | Parks the run on `awaiting_signal` until a signal with that name arrives. With `timeoutMs` the kernel also opens a timer step `${id}:timeout` (`signalTimeoutStepId(id)`); whichever fires first reaches the reducer and the kernel cancels the other. |
| `cmd.awaitHuman(signal, { id, timeoutMs?, context? })` | *array* | Sugar: an `await_signal` with `id` and `timeoutMs`, plus an `emit` on channel `"human"` when `context` is set. Spread it into the command list. See [signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md). |
| `cmd.emit(channel, data)` | `emit` | Side channel. Not journaled: broadcast to the host's `events` emitter and to open SSE streams as `event: emit`. |
| `cmd.complete(output)` | `complete` | Ends the run as `completed` with `output`. |
| `cmd.continueAsNew(input)` | `continue_as_new` | Ends the run as `continued`, journals `input` on a `continue` marker, and the host starts a successor run of the same workflow with that input in the same transaction. The two are linked by `continued_from` / `continued_to`; a parent is notified once, by the run that finally closes. |

Rules the kernel enforces on a reduction:

* At most one `complete` or `continue_as_new`, and no command after it.
* An explicit `id` must be non-empty and not already open on this run.
* Default step ids are `task#N`, `timer#N`, `child#N`, `signal#N`, where `N` is a
  run-wide counter over every step ever opened.

Step ids are how a reducer tells results apart. Give a step an explicit `id` whenever you
fan out or need to recognise the reply later (`event.step_id`).

There is no `cmd.fail`. A run fails when its reducer throws — see
[Failing a run](#failing-a-run).

## The `sequence` helper

For linear pipelines, `sequence([...phases])` compiles to the same `WorkflowDef` a
hand-written reducer produces. Phases run in order; `state.phase` is the index in flight.

```ts
import {
  defineWorkflow, fanOut, fanOutResultsOf, resultOf, sequence, signalOf, sleep, step, waitFor,
} from "@oona/vlo";
import { approve, finish, plan, work } from "./activities.ts";

export const exampleWorkflow = defineWorkflow(
  "example",
  sequence([
    step(plan),
    fanOut(
      work,
      (state) => resultOf(state, plan).items.map((item) => ({ item })),
      { concurrency: 2 },
    ),
    waitFor(approve, { timeoutMs: 86_400_000, onTimeout: "fail" }),
    step(finish, (state) => ({
      uppers: fanOutResultsOf(state, work).map((o) => o.upper),
      approvedBy: signalOf(state, approve).by,
    })),
  ]),
);
```

| Phase | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `step(activity, mapInput?, { id?, when?, onFailure? })` | One task. Input is `mapInput(state)` when given; otherwise the workflow input for phase 0, and the previous phase's stored value afterwards (skipping `sleep`s). `id` pins the step id (default `task#n`). `when(state)` returning `false` stores `null` and skips the task. |
| `fanOut(activity, select, { concurrency, onFailure? })` | One task per item from `select(state)`, at most `concurrency` in flight, step ids `${activity}#${index}`. `select` must be pure: it is re-evaluated on every event. An empty selection stores `[]` and moves on. |
| `fanOutRuns(workflow, select, { concurrency, onFailure? })` | One **child run** per item from `select(state)` (each item is the child's start input), at most `concurrency` in flight, step ids `${workflow}#${index}`. Stores a `ChildResult { status, output, child_run_id }` per item; read with `fanOutRunsResultsOf`. Same purity rule and empty-selection behaviour as `fanOut`. |
| `waitFor(signal, { timeoutMs?, onTimeout?, context? })` | Parks until the signal arrives (step id `wait#<phase>`). With `timeoutMs`, a deadline timer `wait#<phase>:timeout` races it: `onTimeout: "fail"` (default) fails the run, `"continue"` stores `null` and advances. `context` is emitted on the `human` channel. |
| `sleep(ms)` | Parks on a timer (step id `sleep#<phase>`). Stores nothing. |

State shape (`SeqState`): `{ phase, input, results, signals, fan?, usage? }`. Step, fanOut
and fanOutRuns outputs land in `results[name]`; signal payloads in `signals[signalName]`.
Two phases using the same name share a key. `usage` is the run's banked usage as of the last
event (`event.usage_total`), so a charge step can read `state.usage?.tokens`. After the last
phase the run completes with `results`, or with `output(state)` when
`sequence(steps, { output })` is given.

**Failure tolerance.** A task or child that did not succeed throws `WorkflowFailure`, which
fails the run — unless its phase says `onFailure: "continue"`: a `step` then stores `null`,
a `fanOut` stores `null` for that item, and a `fanOutRuns` records the child's `status` with
a `null` output. `null` is also what `when: false` and a `waitFor` `onTimeout: "continue"`
store, so narrow it yourself when those options are in play. Events that do not belong to
the current phase (a late deadline, a duplicate delivery, a signal nobody is waiting for, a
failed task from a phase already left behind) are ignored: same state, no commands.

## Child runs

`cmd.spawn(childWorkflow, input, { id? })` opens a `child` step and creates a run of
`childWorkflow` with `parent_run_id` and `parent_step_id` set. The child's `run_id` is
derived deterministically by the kernel. The child workflow must be registered on the same
host, otherwise the parent's reducer fails.

```ts
on: {
  started: (state) => [state, [cmd.spawn(render, { clip: state.clip }, { id: "render" })]],
  child_done: (state, event) =>
    event.step_id === "render" && event.status === "succeeded"
      ? [state, [cmd.complete(event.output ?? null)]]
      : [state, [cmd.complete(null)]],
}
```

The dispatcher starts the child on its next tick and, when the child reaches a terminal
status, delivers `child_done` to the parent with `status` (`succeeded` for `completed`,
`failed`, or `cancelled`) and the child's `output`. The event carries no error text; a
failed child's reason is on its own `RunView.error` (`client.get(child_run_id)`).

In a `sequence`, `fanOutRuns` does the spawning and the `child_done` bookkeeping for you —
see [the `sequence` helper](#the-sequence-helper).

## Failing a run

Throw `WorkflowFailure(message, details?)` — or anything else — from a handler:

```ts
import { WorkflowFailure } from "@oona/vlo";

task_done: (state, event) => {
  if (event.status !== "succeeded") {
    throw new WorkflowFailure(`${event.activity} ${event.status}`, { step_id: event.step_id });
  }
  …
}
```

The host catches the throw, appends a `fail` marker (`cause: "app_error"`, `error` = the
message, the event that was being folded as the payload) and marks the run `failed`. The
checkpoint from before that event is kept. The message is surfaced as `RunView.error`
(with `cause`) on `GET /v1/runs/{id}`, so a caller can show why the run stopped without
reading the journal.

## Determinism

A handler may read only its arguments. In particular:

* No `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `fetch`, timers or environment. Use `event.ts_ms` and
  `event.random` when you need time or entropy.
* Do the non-deterministic work in an activity and read its output from `task_done`.
* Budgets are decisions over `event.usage_total`, not over a tally you keep.
* Expect at-least-once delivery: ignore an event you are not waiting for instead of acting
  on it twice. `sequence` and `agentLoop` do this by checking `step_id` and phase.

Nothing enforces these rules yet: a reducer is a plain function, and no lint or sandbox
stops it from reading the clock. A mistake is caught when a run is rebuilt from its
journal, as described next.

The host verifies the checkpoint's hash every time it loads one. If the checkpoint is
missing, or was written by a different workflow digest, it folds the journal from seq 0
and compares every transition's `state_hash` with the one journaled on that event. Any
mismatch appends a `nondeterminism` marker with `cause: "nondeterminism_detected"` and fails
the run. Changing a reducer's logic under a live run therefore surfaces as a failed run,
not as silently different state.

## Testing a reducer

`Workflow.reduce(stateJson, event, initInput?)` runs one handler with no host, journal or
kernel. Pass `initInput` for `started`; pass the previous `state` string afterwards.

```ts
const begun = exampleWorkflow.reduce(
  null,
  { type: "started", ts_ms: 1, random: "0".repeat(32), input: { n: 1 }, usage_total: NONE },
  { n: 1 },
);
const next = exampleWorkflow.reduce(begun.state, {
  type: "task_done", ts_ms: 2, random: "0".repeat(32), step_id: "task#1", attempt: 1,
  activity: "example.plan", status: "succeeded", output: { items: ["a"] },
  usage: NONE, usage_total: NONE,
});
// next.state is JSON text; next.commands is the Command[] the handler returned.
```

`NONE` is `{ cpu_ms: 0, tokens: 0, cost_micro_usd: 0 }`. End-to-end tests on an in-process
host, and tests for agents, are covered in [testing.md](./testing.md). The reference tests in
[`../sdk/ts/sdk/test/human.test.ts`](../sdk/ts/sdk/test/human.test.ts) are written this way.
