url: /vlo/activities-and-workers.md
---
# Activities and workers

An **activity** declares a unit of non-deterministic work. A **worker** implements it. The
host sits between them: it validates inputs when a reducer asks for a task, validates
outputs when a worker reports one, and owns leases, retries and idempotency.

## Declaring an activity

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { activity } from "@oona/vlo";

export const work = activity("example.work", {
  input: z.object({ item: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ upper: z.string() }),
  retry: { maxAttempts: 3, backoff: "exponential", initialMs: 1_000, maxMs: 600_000, factor: 2, jitter: "full" },
  queue: "default",
  leaseMs: 60_000,
  timeoutMs: 120_000,
});
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input`, `output` | required | Zod schemas. Input is checked in `cmd.task`; output is checked by the host before the result is folded. |
| `retry.maxAttempts` | `3` | Total attempts. Retrying stops once `attempt >= maxAttempts`. |
| `retry.backoff` | `"exponential"` | `"fixed"` or `"exponential"`. |
| `retry.initialMs` | `1000` | Delay before attempt 2. |
| `retry.maxMs` | `600000` | Cap on the delay. |
| `retry.factor` | `2` | Multiplier per attempt. |
| `retry.jitter` | `"full"` | `"full"` picks a delay uniformly in `[0, base]` using the journaled `random`; `"none"` uses `base`. |
| `queue` | `"default"` | Which queue the task lands on. `cmd.task(…, { queue })` overrides per call. |
| `leaseMs` | `60000` | How long a worker holds an attempt before it must heartbeat. |
| `timeoutMs` | none | Wall-clock budget for one attempt. |

The delay for attempt `n` is `initialMs × factor^(n−2)` capped at `maxMs`, then jittered.
`schema_violation`, `user_cancel` and `nondeterminism_detected` are never retried.

### Changing the ask on a retry

A retry repeats the journaled input. When repeating the same ask would fail the same way —
a model looping inside a long prompt — wrap the handler with `withRetryInput`:

```ts
import { defineWorker, withRetryInput } from "@oona/vlo";

defineWorker({
  "brand.synthesize": withRetryInput(synthesize, (input, attempt) => ({ ...input, compact: attempt > 1 })),
});
```

Attempts after the first receive `shape(input, attempt)`. The journaled task input is
untouched and `attempt` is journaled, so the same attempt always sees the same input, and
nothing about replay changes. `shape` must be pure; its result is not re-validated against
the input schema. This lives on the worker rather than on `activity()` because workers
never see activity definitions (a pushed or pulled task carries only `{ name, schema_ref }`)
and `retry` is part of the content hash, where a function cannot go.

### What is in the content hash

`activity()` hashes `{ v, name, input, output, retry }` and exposes it as `hash` and
`schemaRef` (`name@hash`). `input` and `output` are the JSON Schemas *projected* by
`projectSchema`: annotation keywords (`$schema`, `$id`, `$comment`, `title`, `description`,
`examples`, `default`, `deprecated`, `readOnly`, `writeOnly`) are removed at every depth,
so a `.describe()` label or a `.default()` never re-versions an activity under live runs.
Anything that changes which values a schema accepts (`additionalProperties`, `enum`,
`minimum`, `anyOf`, …) stays in the hash. `v` is `SCHEMA_HASH_VERSION`; it moves only when
the projection rule itself changes. The `schema_ref` travels on every task and event, so a
run can span a schema change. `queue`, `leaseMs` and `timeoutMs` are deliberately outside
the hash: they are operational knobs, and tuning them must not version the schema under
live runs.

Signals hash `{ v, name, schema }` the same way. Every hash is registered in the journal's
`schemas` table when a host boots, with the *full* schema, annotations included, so forms
and validation see the descriptions the hash ignores.

The projection and the encoding are a protocol, not an SDK detail: an SDK in another
language must produce the same `schema_ref` for the same definition. The golden cases in
`fixtures/schema-hash/` are the contract; see
[kernel-protocol.md](./kernel-protocol.md#schema-hash).

## Implementing a worker

```ts
import { defineWorker } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineWorker(
  {
    "example.work": async (input: { item: string }, ctx) => {
      ctx.reportUsage({ tokens: 120, costMicroUsd: 5 });
      return { upper: input.item.toUpperCase() };
    },
  },
  { queues: ["default"] },
);
```

`defineWorker(impls, { queues? })` maps activity names to handlers and says which queues
this process serves (default `["default"]`). The worker holds no schemas; the host validates.

### `TaskContext`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.taskId` | `run_id:step_id`. |
| `ctx.runId` | The run the task belongs to. |
| `ctx.attempt` | 1-based attempt number. |
| `ctx.heartbeat()` | Extends the lease. Rejects once the lease is gone. Called for you every `max(1 s, leaseMs / 3)` while the handler runs; a refused heartbeat aborts `ctx.signal`. |
| `ctx.reportUsage({ tokens?, costMicroUsd?, cpuMs? })` | Accumulates spend for this attempt. Values are truncated to non-negative integers. Banked on success *and* failure, and surfaced to the reducer as `event.usage` and `event.usage_total`. |
| `ctx.signal` | `AbortSignal`. Aborted when the lease is lost, `timeoutMs` elapses, or the worker shuts down. |

A handler's return value must satisfy the activity's `output` schema. A throw fails the
attempt with `cause: "app_error"` and the retry policy decides what happens next.

### Outcomes of one attempt

| What happened | Recorded as | Retried? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Handler returned a valid output | `succeeded` | — |
| Handler returned something the output schema rejects | `failed`, `schema_violation` | never |
| Handler threw | `failed` or `retrying`, `app_error` | per policy |
| `timeoutMs` elapsed (worker-side) | `timeout` | per policy |
| No heartbeat before the lease lapsed (host-side reaper) | `heartbeat_lost` | per policy |
| `dispatched_at + timeoutMs` passed and the worker never answered (host-side backstop) | `timeout` | per policy |
| No handler registered for the activity | `failed` | never |

Exactly one terminal result is accepted per attempt. A timeout, a throw and a late return
race for the same attempt; the first report wins and the others are dropped. A result for an
attempt that has already moved on returns `{ duplicate: true }` and changes nothing.

## Where workers run

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant W as Worker host
  O->>W: POST /v1/tasks/push (vlo-signature, vlo-task-id, vlo-attempt, vlo-timestamp)
  W-->>O: 202 Accepted
  W->>W: run handler, heartbeat every lease/3
  W->>O: POST {complete_url}/complete {attempt, output, usage?}
```

### In-process

A worker exported from a module matched by `workers` (or any module the config loads) runs
inside the host when the host holds `worker:<queue>` for one of its queues. This is what
`vlo dev` does with no queue configuration.

### Push mode (default for remote queues)

The orchestrator's profile names the queue's URL and a shared secret:

```ts
queues: { llm: { url: "https://workers.example.com/v1/tasks/push", secret: env("VLO_PUSH_SECRET") } },
publicUrl: "https://vlo.example.com",
```

The worker side is another host holding the `worker:<queue>` role:

```ts
import { serve } from "@oona/vlo/host";

await serve({
  journal: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
  workflows: [],
  workers: [llmWorker],
  roles: ["worker:llm"],
  auth: { pushSecret: process.env.VLO_PUSH_SECRET!, callbackToken: process.env.VLO_TOKEN! },
  port: 8080,
});
```

The push is a `POST` whose body is the `PushedTask` JSON:

```json
{ "task_id": "run_…:task#1", "run_id": "run_…", "step_id": "task#1", "attempt": 1,
  "activity": { "name": "example.work", "schema_ref": "example.work@…" },
  "idempotency_key": "run_…:task#1:1", "input": { "item": "a" },
  "lease_ms": 60000, "heartbeat_ms": 20000, "timeout_ms": 120000,
  "complete_url": "https://vlo.example.com/v1/tasks/run_…%3Atask%231" }
```

Headers: `vlo-task-id`, `vlo-attempt`, `vlo-timestamp` (epoch ms) and
`vlo-signature: v1=<hex>` where the hex is
`HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<task_id>.<attempt>.<timestamp>.<sha256(body)>")`. The receiver
rejects a timestamp more than 5 minutes off. `verifySignature(secret, headers, rawBody)`
and `signPush(...)` in `@oona/vlo/host` implement both sides.

How the orchestrator reads the worker's answer:

| Response | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `202` | Accepted; the result comes later on `complete_url`. |
| `200 { "output": … }` | Accepted, with the result inline. |
| `409` | Already seen (same `idempotency_key` in flight). Treated as accepted. |
| `401`, `403`, `408`, `429`, any `5xx`, timeout (5 s), socket error | Not now: deferred with backoff `1 s × 2^attempts`, capped at 60 s. |
| any other `4xx` | The worker rejected the task itself: failed with `schema_violation`, not retried. |

A worker written in any language does the same: verify the signature, answer `202`, then
call back on `complete_url` with a bearer token (`auth.token` of the orchestrator):

| Route | Body |
| --- | --- |
| `POST {complete_url}/complete` | `{ "attempt": 1, "output": …, "usage"?: { "tokens", "cost_micro_usd", "cpu_ms" } }` |
| `POST {complete_url}/fail` | `{ "attempt": 1, "error": "…", "retryable"?: true, "cause"?: "timeout", "usage"?: … }` |
| `POST {complete_url}/heartbeat` | `{ "attempt": 1 }` |

`complete_url` is only filled when the orchestrator knows its own `publicUrl`; without it a
pull worker falls back to its configured `baseUrl`.

### Pull mode

Set `mode: "pull"` on the queue and the dispatcher leaves its tasks alone. A worker asks:

```ts
import { runPullWorker } from "@oona/vlo/host";

await runPullWorker({
  baseUrl: "https://vlo.example.com",
  token: process.env.VLO_TOKEN,
  worker: mediaWorker,
  queues: ["media"],   // default: the worker's own queues
  waitMs: 20_000,      // long-poll hold; the host caps it at 25 s
  concurrency: 4,
  signal: controller.signal,
  onError: (error) => console.error(error),
});
```

Under the hood: `POST /v1/tasks/poll` with `{ queue, worker_id, wait_ms, max }` (max ≤ 10)
returns `{ tasks: PushedTask[] }`, already marked `running` with a lease. The host wakes an
open poll the moment a task for that queue is committed in the same process. Results go
back through the same three verbs. The loop backs off 1 s after a failed poll and resolves
after `signal` aborts once in-flight tasks have reported.

## Idempotency

Execution is at-least-once; recording is exactly-once.

* `task_id = run_id:step_id`; `idempotency_key = run_id:step_id:attempt`. A retry is a
  new attempt with a new key; a re-push of the same attempt carries the same key.
* The push route answers `409` while a key is in flight in that process. Across processes,
  or after a crash, a handler may run twice for one key: make it idempotent on
  `ctx.taskId + ctx.attempt` when the side effect matters.
* The first terminal result for an attempt wins; later ones are `{ duplicate: true }`.

## Leases, heartbeats and timeouts

* The lease starts at dispatch (`lease_until = now + leaseMs`). The SDK worker heartbeats
  automatically; a handler only needs `ctx.heartbeat()` if it runs somewhere the SDK is not.
* The orchestrator's reaper fails any `running` attempt whose lease lapsed with
  `heartbeat_lost`. Because heartbeats are automatic, this only happens when the worker
  process is gone, not when a handler is slow.
* `timeoutMs` is enforced twice: the worker aborts the handler (`ctx.signal`) and reports
  `cause: "timeout"`; the orchestrator reaps an attempt past `dispatched_at + timeout_ms`
  in case the worker never answers. Long tasks that should not be cut off simply leave
  `timeoutMs` unset and rely on the lease.
* `SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS` (5 s): on `host.stop()` in-process handlers get this long to report
  before the journal closes.

---

---
url: /vlo/signals-and-humans.md
---
# Signals and humans

A signal is a durable message into a run. A human is a signal: a parked run holds no
compute while it waits, and resumes the moment the reply lands.

## Declaring a signal

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { signal } from "@oona/vlo";

export const approve = signal("example.approve", z.object({ by: z.string() }));
```

`signal(name, schema)` returns a `SignalDef` with `name`, `hash`, `schemaRef`
(`name@hash`) and `schema`. Register it on the host (`signals: [approve]` in `createHost`,
or export it from a module the config loads) and the host validates every incoming payload
against it; an invalid payload is a `400`. An unregistered name is accepted as opaque JSON.

## Waiting for one

```ts
on: {
  started: (state) => [state, [cmd.awaitSignal(approve, { id: "gate", timeoutMs: 3_600_000 })]],
  signal: (state, event) =>
    event.step_id === "gate"
      ? [{ ...state, approvedBy: (event.payload as { by: string }).by }, [cmd.complete(null)]]
      : [state, []],
}
```

`cmd.awaitSignal(def, { id?, timeoutMs? })` opens a `signal` step and moves the run to
`awaiting_signal`. When a matching signal arrives the reducer gets a `signal` event with
`step_id`, `name` and `payload`.

Buffering: a signal that arrives before any wait is open is stored and delivered as soon as
a wait with that name opens. The `POST` reports `delivered: false` in that case, and also
when the matching wait has already closed (its deadline fired, or the run ended): such a
late signal is recorded but never reaches the reducer.

In a `sequence`, use `waitFor`:

```ts
sequence([
  step(plan),
  waitFor(approve, { timeoutMs: 86_400_000, onTimeout: "continue", context: { ask: "approve?" } }),
  step(finish, (state) => ({ approvedBy: signalOf(state, approve)?.by ?? "nobody" })),
])
```

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `timeoutMs` | Races the wait against a deadline timer the kernel opens as `<id>:timeout`. |
| `onTimeout: "fail"` (default) | The deadline fails the run with `human timeout: <name>`. |
| `onTimeout: "continue"` | The deadline stores `null` under `signals[name]` and advances. |
| `context` | Emitted on the `human` channel so a UI can render the ask. |

Whichever arrives first wins and the kernel cancels the loser in the same transition, so
the reducer sees exactly one of the two. A signal that arrives after the deadline is not
delivered (`delivered: false`); a timer row left behind by a delivered signal is retired
by the dispatcher without reaching the reducer.

## `cmd.awaitHuman`

`waitFor` is built on `cmd.awaitHuman(def, { id, timeoutMs?, context? })`, which returns an
array of commands to spread into a reduction:

1. `await_signal` with step id `id` and `timeoutMs`, so the kernel opens the deadline timer
   `${id}:timeout` (`signalTimeoutStepId(id)` builds that string);
2. `emit("human", { signal, id, context })` when `context` is given.

```ts
started: (state) => [state, [...cmd.awaitHuman(approve, { id: "ask", timeoutMs: 60_000, context: { cut: state.cut } })]],
timer: (state, event) =>
  event.step_id === "ask:timeout" ? [state, [cmd.complete({ approved: false })]] : [state, []],
```

The `human` emit is not journaled. It reaches listeners on the host's `events` emitter and
any open SSE stream (`event: emit`). A client that connects later reads the run's status
(`awaiting_signal`) and the signal wait from the journal instead.

## Delivering a signal

```sh
curl -X POST https://vlo.example.com/v1/runs/run_…/signals/example.approve \
  -H 'authorization: Bearer …' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"by":"dc"}'
# {"signal_id":"sig_…","delivered":true}
```

```ts
const result = await client.signal(runId, approve, { by: "dc" });
// result.delivered is false when the signal was buffered
```

`client.signal(runId, nameOrDef, payload)` accepts a string or a `SignalDef`. Signals are
accepted while the run is `running` too: they buffer until the next wait opens.

An inbox is a query: `GET /v1/runs?status=awaiting_signal` (or
`client.list({ status: "awaiting_signal" })`).

## Signed links

A signed link is a URL that delivers one named signal to one run without a bearer token —
the thing you put in an email or a chat message.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Your app
  participant H as Host
  participant P as Person
  A->>H: POST /v1/runs/{id}/links/approve (bearer)
  H-->>A: { url: "…/signals/approve?token=v1.<exp>.<hmac>", expires_at_ms }
  A->>P: email the url
  P->>H: GET url
  H-->>P: confirmation form (nothing changes)
  P->>H: POST url (form submit)
  H-->>P: { delivered: true }
```

### Minting

```ts
const link = await client.signalLink(runId, approve, { expiresInMs: 86_400_000 });
// { url: "https://vlo.example.com/v1/runs/run_…/signals/example.approve?token=v1.1760000000000.9f…", expires_at_ms: 1760000000000 }
```

`POST /v1/runs/{id}/links/{name}` with an optional body `{ "expires_in_ms": N }` (default 7
days) requires the bearer token. The URL is built from the host's `publicUrl` (falling back
to the request origin) and `basePath`.

Token format: `v1.<expires_at_ms>.<hmac>` with
`hmac = HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<run_id>.<name>.<expires_at_ms>")` in hex. It authorises
exactly that `(run, signal)` pair until that instant; a leaked token cannot start a run,
read a journal or signal anything else.

### Secret

Links are signed with `auth.linkSecret`, falling back to `auth.token`, then
`auth.pushSecret`. With none of the three configured, minting answers `503 links_disabled`.
`linkSecret` and `callbackToken` are `createHost` options; the config-file profile only
carries `token` and `pushSecret`.

### Using the link

* `GET …/signals/{name}?token=…` renders a small HTML confirmation form and changes
  nothing, so mail scanners and link previews cannot signal a run. The form POSTs the same
  URL.
* `POST …/signals/{name}?token=…` delivers the signal. The body is the payload; a browser
  form sends none, so a signal meant for links needs a schema that accepts an empty payload
  (`z.unknown()`, or an object with only optional fields).
* A tampered, expired or wrong-pair token falls through to the bearer check and gets the
  same `401` as no credential at all.

## Client summary

| Method | Route |
| --- | --- |
| `client.signal(runId, name, payload)` | `POST /v1/runs/{id}/signals/{name}` |
| `client.signalLink(runId, name, { expiresInMs? })` | `POST /v1/runs/{id}/links/{name}` |
| `client.list({ status: "awaiting_signal" })` | `GET /v1/runs?status=awaiting_signal` |
| `client.waitFor(runId, "awaiting_signal")` | polls `GET /v1/runs/{id}` |

See [http-api.md](./http-api.md) for the full route reference.

url: /vlo/agent-harness.md
---
# Build an agent harness

An agent harness is the code around a model: it calls the model, runs the tools the model
picks, keeps memory, enforces a budget and waits for people. This guide builds one on Vlo
and shows what the engine gives you for free.

| A harness has to | On Vlo |
| --- | --- |
| Survive a crash on step 40 | Every decision, tool call and score is one journaled event. The run continues from the last one. |
| Stop a runaway agent | The kernel meters tokens and cost on every event. A spent budget parks the run. |
| Not lose work when it stops | A parked run keeps its memory and its best result, and resumes on a top-up. |
| Ask before a risky action | A gated tool waits for a person's yes or no. The run holds no compute while it waits. |
| Cope with bad model output | An unknown tool or invalid arguments becomes an observation, and the model decides again. |
| Run tools wherever they live | A tool is an activity. Its worker can be in-process, a serverless function or a Python service. |
| Show what happened | The journal is the trace: every step, retry and token is a row. |

The reference for every option is [agents.md](./agents.md).

**Everything on this page is runnable.** The code is
[`../examples/harness/`](../examples/harness/), which uses a scripted model so it needs no
API key. It is typechecked and tested in CI. From a checkout:

```sh
pnpm install                       # once, from the repository root
cd examples && pnpm dev:harness    # API on :4100
```

## How the loop works

`agentLoop` builds a decide → tool → evaluate loop as a reducer. Nothing loops at runtime:
each arrow below is one event folded into state.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S([start: goal]) --> D[decide: the model picks a tool]
  D -->|tool| T[tool: a worker runs it]
  D -->|gated tool| A[wait for a person]
  A -->|approved| T
  A -->|rejected| B
  D -->|done| F([complete])
  T --> E[evaluate: score the result]
  E -->|"score ≥ threshold"| F
  E -->|below| B{budget left?}
  B -->|yes| D
  B -->|no| P[park until a top-up]
  P -->|top-up signal| D
```

## 1. Declare the tools

A tool is an ordinary activity with typed input and output. `activities.ts`:

```ts
export const search = activity("research.search", {
  input: z.object({ query: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ results: z.array(z.string()) }),
});

export const write = activity("research.write", {
  input: z.object({ notes: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
});

export const publish = activity("research.publish", {
  input: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ url: z.string() }),
});

export const evaluate = activity("research.evaluate", {
  input: z.object({ goal: z.unknown(), candidate: z.unknown() }),
  output: z.object({ score: z.number() }),
});
```

`search` and `write` are safe to run unattended. `publish` reaches the outside world, so
step 3 puts a person in front of it.

## 2. Declare the decision

`decision` is the activity behind which your model call lives. Its output is fixed by the
tool registry, so the model can only name a tool the loop can run, or `"done"`.

```ts
export const decide = decision("research.decide", {
  input: z.object({
    goal: z.unknown(),
    memory: z.array(z.unknown()),
    candidate: z.unknown(),
    score: z.unknown(),
  }),
  tools: { search, write, publish },
});

export const topup = budgetTopup();
```

The decision returns `{ tool, args?, rationale?, final? }`.

## 3. Build the loop

`research.workflow.ts`:

```ts
import { defineWorkflow } from "@oona/vlo";
import { agentLoop } from "@oona/vlo/agent";
import { decide, evaluate, publish, search, topup, write } from "./activities.ts";

export default defineWorkflow(
  "research",
  agentLoop({
    decide,
    tools: { search, write, publish },
    evaluate,
    threshold: 0.9,
    budget: { tokens: 50_000, costMicroUsd: 2_000_000 },
    topup,
    approval: { tools: ["publish"], timeoutMs: 172_800_000 },
    maxIterations: 30,
  }),
);
```

That is the whole agent:

* `budget` is the ceiling on what one run may spend.
* `threshold` is the score at which the run completes on its own.
* `approval` names the tools that wait for a person. Here a request that nobody answers in
  two days counts as a no.

## 4. Put the model in a worker

The worker is where the model call happens. Report what each call spent, so the budget
means something. `research.worker.ts`:

```ts
import { defineWorker } from "@oona/vlo";
import { decideNext, grade, post, webSearch, writeReport, type DecideInput } from "./model.ts";

export default defineWorker({
  "research.decide": async (input: DecideInput, ctx) => {
    const reply = await decideNext(input);
    ctx.reportUsage({ tokens: reply.tokens, costMicroUsd: reply.costMicroUsd });
    return { tool: reply.tool, args: reply.args ?? null, rationale: reply.why };
  },

  "research.search": async (input: { query: string }) => ({
    results: await webSearch(input.query),
  }),

  "research.write": async (input: { notes: string }, ctx) => {
    const reply = await writeReport(input.notes);
    ctx.reportUsage({ tokens: reply.tokens, costMicroUsd: reply.costMicroUsd });
    return { text: reply.text };
  },

  "research.publish": async (input: { text: string }) => ({
    url: await post(input.text),
  }),

  "research.evaluate": async (input: { goal: unknown; candidate: unknown }) => ({
    score: await grade(input.goal, input.candidate),
  }),
});
```

`decideNext`, `writeReport`, `webSearch`, `post` and `grade` live in
[`model.ts`](../examples/harness/model.ts). In the example they are scripted stand-ins; in
your harness they are your model client and your tools. Vlo does not ship a model client
and has no price table: `costMicroUsd` is whatever you report.

Usage is banked on failed attempts too, so a model call that times out and retries still
counts against the budget.

## 5. Run it

`vlo.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineConfig({
  workflows: ["*.workflow.ts"],
  workers: ["*.worker.ts"],
  activities: ["activities.ts"],
  profiles: {
    dev: {
      journal: "sqlite://.vlo/harness.db",
      blob: "file://.vlo/blobs",
      roles: ["orchestrator", "api", "worker:default"],
      dispatcher: { mode: "loop" },
    },
  },
});
```

```sh
pnpm dev:harness
```

```ts
import { createClient } from "@oona/vlo/host";

const client = createClient({ baseUrl: "http://localhost:4100" });
const run = await client.start("research", { topic: "durable execution" });
```

The run input is the agent's goal. With the scripted model the agent searches, writes a
short report, then asks to publish it and waits. Step 9 answers it.

## 6. Watch it think

Follow the run live. Journal frames are durable, so reconnecting with the last `seq` loses
nothing.

```ts
for await (const message of client.stream(run.run_id)) {
  if (message.type === "journal") console.log(message.seq, message.data.step_id, message.data.status);
  if (message.type === "end") console.log("finished:", message.data.status);
}
```

Step ids tell you where the agent is: `decide#0`, `tool#0`, `evaluate#0`, `decide#1`, and so
on. After the run, `client.events(runId)` returns the same history, including each
attempt's `usage`. See [observability.md](./observability.md).

## 7. When the budget runs out

The run does not fail. Its status becomes `awaiting_signal`, it holds no compute, and it
keeps its memory and its best candidate.

```ts
const parked = await client.waitFor(run.run_id, "awaiting_signal");

// Somebody decides to keep going.
await client.signal(run.run_id, topup, { tokens: 20_000 });
```

* To find every parked run: `client.list({ status: "awaiting_signal" })`.
* To stop instead: `client.cancel(runId)`.
* To let a person approve the extra spend from an email, mint a signed link:
  `client.signalLink(runId, topup)`. See
  [signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md#signed-links).

## 8. When the model misbehaves

The decider is a model, so bad output is an ordinary outcome, not a crash.

| The model | What the loop does |
| --- | --- |
| Names a tool that is not registered | Records the error as an observation and decides again. |
| Sends arguments the tool's schema rejects | Records `invalid args` as an observation and decides again. |
| Picks a tool that fails after its retries | Records the failure as an observation and decides again. |
| Returns no `tool` at all | Fails the run. |

Because each recovery is another iteration, it counts against `budget.steps` and
`maxIterations`. The agent cannot loop on a mistake forever.

## 9. Add a human approval

When the model picks a gated tool, the loop does not run it. The run's status becomes
`awaiting_signal`, it holds no compute, and it waits for a person.

Each gated call waits on its own signal, named after its iteration. The scripted agent asks
to publish on its third cycle, so the wait's step id is `approve#2` and `approvalSignal(2)`
answers it:

```ts
await client.signal(run.run_id, approvalSignal(2), { approved: true, by: "dana" });
```

The tool then runs as usual. To say no instead:

```ts
await client.signal(run.run_id, approvalSignal(2), { approved: false, reason: "not this week" });
```

A rejection is not a failure. The tool does not run, the reason goes into the agent's
memory as an observation, and the model decides what to do next.

To let someone approve from an email or a chat message, mint a signed link. Opening it
changes nothing; confirming the form approves that one call.

```ts
const link = await client.signalLink(run.run_id, approvalSignal(2), { expiresInMs: 86_400_000 });
```

What to know:

* **An approval is single-use.** Because each call has its own signal, a duplicate reply or
  an old link can never approve a later call.
* **To find what is being asked**, read the run's events for the open `approve#<i>` step, or
  listen on the `human` channel of the event stream, which carries the tool, its arguments
  and the model's rationale.
* **A reviewer cannot edit the arguments.** They approve or reject the call as the model
  made it.
* **With `timeoutMs`**, an unanswered request counts as a rejection. Set
  `onTimeout: "fail"` to fail the run instead.

To gate a whole result instead of one tool, run the agent as a child of a pipeline with a
`waitFor`; see [recipes.md](./recipes.md#wait-for-an-approval-with-a-deadline).

## 10. Run agents in parallel

Each agent is a run, so a team of agents is a fan-out of child runs with a concurrency
limit:

```ts
export const agents = fanOutRuns(
  "research",
  (state) => (state.input as { topics: string[] }).topics.map((topic) => ({ topic })),
  { concurrency: 4 },
);
```

Each child has its own journal, its own budget and its own usage total. A parent does not
see what its children spent; read each child's `output.spent`.

## 11. Move the model call off the host

A tool can run somewhere else without changing the workflow. Give the activity a queue and
point the queue at a worker:

```ts
export const decide = decision("research.decide", { input: …, tools: { search, write, publish }, queue: "llm" });
```

```ts
// in the production profile
queues: { llm: { url: env("VLO_QUEUE_LLM_URL"), secret: env("VLO_PUSH_SECRET") } },
```

The worker can be a serverless function that exists only while it works, or a service in
another language that verifies the signature and calls back. See
[activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#where-workers-run).

## What Vlo does not do for you

* **It does not call the model.** Bring your own client and prompts.
* **It does not price tokens.** You report cost; the kernel banks it.
* **It does not manage long context.** The loop keeps the last 20 observations
  (`memoryLimit`) and drops older ones. Summarise in a tool if you need more.
* **It does not roll child usage up to a parent.**

## Next

* [agents.md](./agents.md): every option, the state shape and the result shape.
* [testing.md](./testing.md#testing-an-agent): test the loop with a scripted model and no API key.
* [recipes.md](./recipes.md): short answers to common tasks.

url: /vlo/agents.md

# Agents

`@oona/vlo/agent` builds a decide → tool → evaluate loop that survives crashes, stays inside
a budget and waits for people. It ships inside `@oona/vlo`.

* **An agent survives a crash mid-thought.** Nothing loops at runtime: every arrow in the
  diagram below is one journaled event folded into state. Kill the process and the run
  continues from its last event.
* **A spent budget parks the run instead of failing it.** The kernel banks usage on every
  event, including failed attempts. The run waits for a top-up and keeps what it has done.
* **A risky tool waits for a person.** A gated tool call parks the run until someone says
  yes or no. A no becomes an observation, not a failure.
* **Bad model output is an ordinary outcome.** An unknown tool or invalid arguments becomes
  an observation, and the model decides again.

This page is the reference. For a walkthrough with a model call, approvals and parallel
agents, see [agent-harness.md](./agent-harness.md).

```sh
pnpm add @oona/vlo zod
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S([start: goal, tools, budget]) --> D["decide#i"]
  D -->|tool| T["tool#i"]
  D -->|gated tool| A["awaiting_signal on approve#i"]
  A -->|approved| T
  A -->|"rejected or timed out"| B
  D -->|done| F([complete])
  T --> E["evaluate#i"]
  E -->|"score ≥ threshold"| F
  E -->|below| B{budget left?}
  T -->|no evaluator| B
  B -->|yes| D
  B -->|no| P["awaiting_signal on topup#i"]
  P -->|top-up signal| D
```

## The pieces

### `decision(name, { input, tools, retry?, queue?, timeoutMs? })`

An ordinary activity whose output schema is fixed by the tool registry, so an LLM worker is
constrained to names the loop can dispatch:

```ts
{ tool: "<one of tools>" | "done", args?: unknown, rationale?: string, final?: Json }
```

`"done"` is reserved: a tool named `done` throws at definition time. The worker behind it
is your model call.

### `agentLoop(options)`

Returns a `WorkflowDef<AgentState, Json>`; hand it to `defineWorkflow`.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decide` | required | The decider activity. Receives `{ goal, memory, candidate, score }`. |
| `tools` | required | `Record<string, Activity>`, keyed by the name `decide` returns. |
| `evaluate` | none | Scores a candidate. Receives `{ goal, candidate }`; returns a `number` or `{ score: number }`. |
| `threshold` | none | Score at or above which the run completes. Without one only `decide` can finish. |
| `budget` | required | `{ tokens?, costMicroUsd?, steps? }`. An absent ceiling never binds. |
| `topup` | `budgetTopup()` | The signal a parked agent waits on. |
| `approval` | none | `{ tools, name?, timeoutMs?, onTimeout? }`. Tools that wait for a person before they run. See [Approving tool calls](#approving-tool-calls). |
| `maxIterations` | `50` | Completes with `exhausted: true` when reached. |
| `memoryLimit` | `20` | Observations kept in state; older ones are dropped. |

### `budgetTopup(name = "agent.budget_topup")`

A `SignalDef<{ tokens?, costMicroUsd?, steps? }>`. Each field is added to the matching
ceiling; a ceiling that was never set stays unbounded.

### `approvalSignal(iteration, name = "agent.tool_approval")`

The `SignalDef<{ approved?, reason?, by? }>` that the gated call of `iteration` waits on. Its
name is `<name>:<iteration>`. Pass it to `client.signal` or `client.signalLink`.

## Example

```ts
// agent.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { activity, defineWorkflow } from "@oona/vlo";
import { agentLoop, budgetTopup, decision } from "@oona/vlo/agent";

export const draft = activity("agent.draft", {
  input: z.object({ topic: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
});

export const rewrite = activity("agent.rewrite", {
  input: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
  output: z.object({ text: z.string() }),
});

export const evaluate = activity("agent.evaluate", {
  input: z.object({ goal: z.unknown(), candidate: z.unknown() }),
  output: z.object({ score: z.number() }),
});

export const decide = decision("agent.decide", {
  input: z.object({
    goal: z.unknown(),
    memory: z.array(z.unknown()),
    candidate: z.unknown(),
    score: z.unknown(),
  }),
  tools: { draft, rewrite },
});

export const topup = budgetTopup();

export default defineWorkflow(
  "headline-agent",
  agentLoop({
    decide,
    tools: { draft, rewrite },
    evaluate,
    threshold: 0.9,
    budget: { tokens: 20_000, steps: 12 },
    topup,
    maxIterations: 20,
  }),
);
```

The worker is where the model lives. Report usage so the budget means something:

```ts
import { defineWorker } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineWorker({
  "agent.decide": async (input: { goal: unknown; memory: unknown[] }, ctx) => {
    const reply = await callModel(input);           // your LLM call
    ctx.reportUsage({ tokens: reply.tokens, costMicroUsd: reply.costMicroUsd });
    return reply.memory_is_good_enough
      ? { tool: "done", final: reply.best, rationale: reply.why }
      : { tool: "draft", args: { topic: reply.topic }, rationale: reply.why };
  },
  "agent.draft": async (input: { topic: string }, ctx) => { /* … */ return { text: "…" }; },
  "agent.rewrite": async (input: { text: string }) => ({ text: input.text.trim() }),
  "agent.evaluate": async (input: { candidate: { text: string } }) => ({ score: 0.8 }),
});
```

Register `decide`, `draft`, `rewrite`, `evaluate` as activities and `topup` as a signal on
the host (export them from a module the config loads, or pass `activities` / `signals` to
`createHost`).

## One iteration

Step ids are `decide#i`, `approve#i`, `tool#i`, `evaluate#i` and `topup#i`, where `i` is the
iteration.

1. **decide** — `cmd.task(decide, { goal, memory, candidate, score }, { id: "decide#i" })`.
   `candidate` and `score` are the last tool output and its score, or `null`.
2. On `done`: complete with `final ?? candidate`. Otherwise validate `args` against the
   chosen tool's input schema and dispatch `tool#i`, or wait on `approve#i` first when the
   tool is gated.
3. **tool** — the output becomes `candidate` and an observation
   `{ tool, args, output }` in `memory`. With no `evaluate`, go to step 5.
4. **evaluate** — `cmd.task(evaluate, { goal, candidate }, { id: "evaluate#i" })`. The
   score is written onto that observation. `score >= threshold` completes the run.
5. **advance** — `iteration + 1`. At `maxIterations`, complete with `exhausted: true`. If
   `isExhausted(budget, spent, iteration)`, park. Else decide again.

`spent` is the run's `usage_total` as carried on the last event; the loop never keeps its
own tally. `steps` compares against the iteration count.

### Routing around trouble

The decider is a model, so bad output is an ordinary outcome, not a run failure:

| Situation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Tool task failed after its retries, or was cancelled | Observation `{ tool, error }`; decide again. |
| `decide` named a tool that is not registered | Observation `{ tool, error: 'unknown tool "…"' }`; decide again. |
| `args` fail the tool's input schema | Observation `{ tool, args, error: "invalid args: …" }`; decide again. |
| `decide` output has no string `tool` | `WorkflowFailure` — the run fails. |
| `evaluate` output has no numeric score | `WorkflowFailure` — the run fails. |
| A result for a step the loop is not waiting for | Ignored: same state, no commands. |

## Approving tool calls

```ts
agentLoop({ decide, tools: { search, publish }, budget, approval: { tools: ["publish"], timeoutMs: 86_400_000 } });
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tools` | required | Names of the gated tools. Each must be a key of `tools`; an unknown name throws at definition time. |
| `name` | `"agent.tool_approval"` | Prefix of the signal name. |
| `timeoutMs` | none | How long to wait. Without one the run waits until somebody answers. |
| `onTimeout` | `"reject"` | `"reject"` records `approval timed out` as an observation and decides again. `"fail"` fails the run. |

When `decide` picks a gated tool with valid arguments, the reducer does not dispatch it. It
emits `cmd.awaitHuman(approvalSignal(i, name), { id: "approve#i", timeoutMs, context })`,
where `context` is `{ tool, args, iteration, rationale? }`. The run's status becomes
`awaiting_signal` and it holds no compute.

```ts
import { approvalSignal } from "@oona/vlo/agent";

await client.signal(runId, approvalSignal(3), { approved: true, by: "dana" });
await client.signal(runId, approvalSignal(3), { approved: false, reason: "wrong audience" });
```

| Reply | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `{ approved: true }`, `{}` or no payload | The tool is dispatched as `tool#i`. An empty reply approves so that a signed link's confirmation form is enough. |
| `{ approved: false, reason?, by? }` | Observation `{ tool, args, error: "rejected by …: …" }`; advance and decide again. |
| A payload that is not an approval | Treated as a rejection: `rejected: the approval reply was not valid`. |
| Nothing before `timeoutMs` | Per `onTimeout`. |

Things to know:

* **Each call has its own signal**, `<name>:<i>`. A duplicate reply, a late reply or a signed
  link for one call can never approve another. The names are not registered on the host, so
  there is nothing to add to `signals`.
* **A rejection or a timeout ends the iteration.** It counts against `budget.steps` and
  `maxIterations`, so an agent cannot ask forever.
* **Finding the open request.** The wait is the event with step id `approve#i` and status
  `awaiting_signal`; the `human` emit on the event stream carries the context.
* **The reviewer cannot change the arguments.** The call runs as the decider made it, or not
  at all.
* **A parked budget and a pending approval are both `awaiting_signal`.** Tell them apart by
  the open step id: `topup#i` or `approve#i`.

## Parking and top-ups

When a ceiling is reached the reducer emits
`cmd.emit("agent", { parked: { iteration, budget, spent, candidate, score } })` and
`cmd.awaitSignal(topup, { id: "topup#i" })`. The run's status becomes `awaiting_signal` and
it holds no compute.

```ts
// Somebody decides to keep going.
await client.signal(runId, topup, { tokens: 10_000 });
```

The grant raises the ceilings that were set and the loop decides again. A grant too small
to help parks again on the next iteration under a fresh step id. A top-up that arrives while
the run is not parked is ignored. Cancel the run instead if the answer is "stop":
`client.cancel(runId)`.

Signed links work here too: mint one for `agent.budget_topup` and the form's empty POST
grants nothing but resumes the loop — give the schema a default if you want a link click to
add budget. See [signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md).

## State and result

`AgentState` (journaled as the run's state):

```ts
{ phase: "decide" | "approval" | "tool" | "evaluate" | "parked" | "done", goal, iteration, memory: Observation[],
  candidate?, score?, pending?: { tool, args }, budget, spent: { cpu_ms, tokens, cost_micro_usd } }
```

`AgentResult` (the run's `output`):

```ts
{ candidate: Json, score?: number, iterations: number,
  spent: { cpu_ms, tokens, cost_micro_usd }, exhausted?: true }
```

`iterations` counts the cycle in flight when the loop finished on a verdict; on
`maxIterations` it is the ceiling itself.

Reference: [`../sdk/ts/sdk/test/agent/example.ts`](../sdk/ts/sdk/test/agent/example.ts) and
[`../sdk/ts/sdk/test/agent/e2e.test.ts`](../sdk/ts/sdk/test/agent/e2e.test.ts), and the runnable
[`../examples/agent/`](../examples/agent/).

# Testing

A Vlo workflow is a pure function, so most of it can be tested with no engine, no database
and no network. This page covers three levels. Every test on it is a real file under
[`../examples/`](../examples/) and runs in CI with `pnpm --filter @oona/vlo-examples test`.

| Level | What runs | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Unit](#unit-test-a-reducer) | One call to your reducer | Logic: which commands follow which event. |
| [End to end](#end-to-end-in-process) | A real host on a throwaway SQLite journal, no socket | Whole runs: tasks, signals, retries, parking. |
| [Agent](#testing-an-agent) | The same, with a scripted model | Agent loops, with no API key and no cost. |

## Unit test a reducer

`workflow.reduce(stateJson, event, initInput?)` runs one handler. Pass `initInput` for
`started`; pass the previous `state` string afterwards. This is the test for the
[hello example](../examples/hello/):

```ts
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import workflow from "./hello.workflow.ts";

const NONE = { cpu_ms: 0, tokens: 0, cost_micro_usd: 0 };
const base = { ts_ms: 1, random: "0".repeat(32), usage_total: NONE };

it("asks for a greeting, then completes with it", () => {
  const begun = workflow.reduce(null, { ...base, type: "started", input: { name: "world" } }, { name: "world" });
  expect(begun.commands).toMatchObject([{ type: "task", input: { name: "world" } }]);

  const done = workflow.reduce(begun.state, {
    ...base, type: "task_done", step_id: "task#1", attempt: 1,
    activity: "hello.greet", status: "succeeded", output: { greeting: "Hello, world!" }, usage: NONE,
  });
  expect(done.commands).toEqual([{ type: "complete", output: { greeting: "Hello, world!" } }]);
});

it("fails the run when the greeting fails", () => {
  const begun = workflow.reduce(null, { ...base, type: "started", input: { name: "world" } }, { name: "world" });

  expect(() =>
    workflow.reduce(begun.state, {
      ...base, type: "task_done", step_id: "task#1", attempt: 1,
      activity: "hello.greet", status: "failed", error: "no greeter", usage: NONE,
    }),
  ).toThrow("no greeter");
});
```

`state` is JSON text and `commands` is the list the handler returned. Because the reducer
reads only its arguments, the same input always gives the same output; there is nothing to
mock.

Things worth a unit test:

* the failure path: a `task_done` with `status: "failed"`, as above;
* an event you are not waiting for, which should return the same state and no commands;
* a budget decision, by setting `usage_total` on the event.

## End to end, in process

Start a real host on a temporary SQLite file and talk to it through `host.fetch`, which
skips the socket. Everything else is the real engine: the kernel, the journal, the
dispatcher and your workers. This is the test for the
[pipeline example](../examples/pipeline/):

```ts
import { mkdtemp, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { createClient, createHost, type Host } from "@oona/vlo/host";
import { afterEach, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { approve, finish, plan, work } from "./activities.ts";
import worker from "./pipeline.worker.ts";
import pipeline from "./pipeline.workflow.ts";

let host: Host;
let dir: string;

afterEach(async () => {
  await host.stop();
  await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
});

it("waits for approval, then finishes", async () => {
  dir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "vlo-test-"));
  host = createHost({
    journal: `sqlite://${join(dir, "journal.db")}`,
    blob: `file://${join(dir, "blobs")}`,
    workflows: [pipeline],
    activities: [plan, work, finish],
    signals: [approve],
    workers: [worker],
    dispatcher: { tickMs: 10 },
  });
  await host.start();
  const client = createClient({ fetch: host.fetch });

  const run = await client.start(pipeline, { n: 3 });
  await client.waitFor(run.run_id, "awaiting_signal");

  await client.signal(run.run_id, approve, { by: "test" });
  const done = await client.waitFor(run.run_id, "completed");

  expect(done.output).toMatchObject({
    "pipeline.finish": { report: "ITEM-0,ITEM-1,ITEM-2 approved by test" },
  });
});
```

Notes:

* `dispatcher: { tickMs: 10 }` makes the dispatcher pass often, so tests do not wait for
  the default 500 ms tick.
* `client.waitFor(runId, status, timeoutMs?)` polls until the run reaches a status. The
  default timeout is 10 seconds.
* `client.events(runId)` returns the journal, so a test can assert on exactly which steps
  ran and in what order.
* Use one journal per test. SQLite is single-writer, and a fresh file keeps tests
  independent.

To run the same tests against Postgres, pass a `postgres://` URL as `journal`.

## Testing an agent

Replace the model with a scripted worker: a pure function of the memory it is shown. The
loop, the budget and the parking are all real. This is the decider from the
[agent example](../examples/agent/):

```ts
"agent.decide": (input: { memory: unknown[]; candidate: { text?: string } | null }, ctx) => {
  ctx.reportUsage({ tokens: TOKENS.decide });
  const pass = input.memory.length;
  if (pass === 0) return { tool: "draft", args: { topic: "durable execution" }, rationale: "nothing yet" };
  if (pass === 1 && input.candidate?.text !== undefined) {
    return { tool: "rewrite", args: { text: input.candidate.text }, rationale: "tighten it" };
  }
  return { tool: "done", rationale: "good enough" };
},
```

Its budget is 15 tokens and the first cycle spends 18, so the run parks:

```ts
// The first cycle spends 18 tokens against a budget of 15, so the run parks.
const run = await client.start(agent, { topic: "durable execution" });
await client.waitFor(run.run_id, "awaiting_signal");

await client.signal(run.run_id, topup, { tokens: 100 });
const done = await client.waitFor(run.run_id, "completed");
const result = done.output as unknown as AgentResult;

expect(result.candidate).toEqual({ text: "a polished headline about durable execution" });
expect(result.spent.tokens).toBe(36);
```

Make the scripted decider depend only on its input, never on a counter outside it. A task
can be delivered more than once, and a decider that counts calls would drift.

The harness example tests a longer loop and an approval gate the same way:
[`../examples/harness/harness.test.ts`](../examples/harness/harness.test.ts).

## Testing a journal adapter

If you write your own journal, `journalConformance` from `@oona/vlo/testing` runs the suite
the built-in adapters pass. `fakeClock` from the same entry gives tests a clock they
control. See [journal.md](./journal.md).

## What tests cannot catch yet

Nothing stops a reducer from reading the clock or calling the network, and a unit test
will not notice if it does. An impure reducer is caught only when a run is rebuilt from its
journal. Keep reducers free of `Date`, `Math.random`, `fetch` and environment reads. See
[workflows.md](./workflows.md#determinism).

# Recipes

Short answers to "how do I…". Each recipe links to the page with the full detail. The
TypeScript on this page is typechecked in CI: it is copied from
[`../examples/recipes/recipes.ts`](../examples/recipes/recipes.ts).

| I want to | Recipe |
| --- | --- |
| Wait for a person | [Wait for an approval, with a deadline](#wait-for-an-approval-with-a-deadline) |
| Approve from an email | [Send an approval link](#send-an-approval-link) |
| Make an agent ask before acting | [Approve a tool call](#approve-a-tool-call) |
| Limit what an agent spends | [Cap an agent's spend](#cap-an-agents-spend) |
| Limit what a pipeline spends | [Stop a pipeline when it has spent too much](#stop-a-pipeline-when-it-has-spent-too-much) |
| Call a flaky model or API | [Retry a flaky call](#retry-a-flaky-call) |
| Run something for hours | [Run a task for hours](#run-a-task-for-hours) |
| Process many items | [Fan out, narrow or wide](#fan-out-narrow-or-wide) |
| Keep going when one step fails | [Tolerate a failure](#tolerate-a-failure) |
| Show progress in a UI | [Stream progress to a UI](#stream-progress-to-a-ui) |
| Avoid starting the same work twice | [Start a run idempotently](#start-a-run-idempotently) |
| Wait, then continue | [Sleep or wait until a time](#sleep-or-wait-until-a-time) |
| Write a worker in Python or Go | [Write a worker in another language](#write-a-worker-in-another-language) |
| Run a worker behind a firewall | [Pull tasks instead of receiving pushes](#pull-tasks-instead-of-receiving-pushes) |
| Keep a run going for months | [Compact a very long run](#compact-a-very-long-run) |
| Stop a run | [Cancel a run](#cancel-a-run) |

## Wait for an approval, with a deadline

```ts
export const approve = signal("order.approve", z.object({ by: z.string() }));

export const order = sequence([
  step(prepare),
  waitFor(approve, { timeoutMs: 86_400_000, onTimeout: "fail" }),
  step(ship, (state) => ({ approvedBy: signalOf(state, approve).by })),
]);
```

Deliver the approval with `client.signal(runId, approve, { by: "dana" })`. The run holds no
compute while it waits. Use `onTimeout: "continue"` to carry on without an answer; the
signal value is then `null`. See [signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md).

## Send an approval link

```ts
const link = await client.signalLink(runId, approve, { expiresInMs: 86_400_000 });
await sendEmail({ to: reviewer, body: `Approve here: ${link.url}` });
```

Opening the link shows a confirmation form and changes nothing, so mail scanners cannot
approve by accident. A browser form sends no payload, so give a signal meant for links a
schema that accepts an empty one (optional fields, or `z.unknown()`). See
[signals-and-humans.md](./signals-and-humans.md#signed-links).

## Approve a tool call

Name the tools that need a person's yes:

```ts
export const careful = agentLoop({
  decide,
  tools,
  budget: { tokens: 50_000 },
  approval: { tools: ["search"], timeoutMs: 86_400_000 },
});
```

When the model picks one, the run waits and holds no compute. Each call waits on its own
signal, named after its iteration; the wait's step id is `approve#<i>`. Answer it either
way:

```ts
await client.signal(runId, approvalSignal(3), { approved: true, by: "dana" });
await client.signal(runId, approvalSignal(3), { approved: false, reason: "wrong audience" });
```

A rejection becomes an observation and the model decides again. To approve from an email,
mint a link for that one call:

```ts
const link = await client.signalLink(runId, approvalSignal(3));
await sendEmail({ to: reviewer, body: `The agent wants to search. Approve: ${link.url}` });
```

See [agents.md](./agents.md#approving-tool-calls).

## Cap an agent's spend

```ts
export const capped = agentLoop({
  decide,
  tools,
  budget: { tokens: 50_000, costMicroUsd: 2_000_000, steps: 25 },
  topup,
});
```

Report usage from each worker with `ctx.reportUsage({ tokens, costMicroUsd })`. When a
ceiling is reached the run parks on `awaiting_signal` and keeps its work. Resume it with
`client.signal(runId, topup, { tokens: 20_000 })`. See [agents.md](./agents.md#parking-and-top-ups).

## Stop a pipeline when it has spent too much

Every event carries the run's banked usage, and `sequence` keeps it in `state.usage`. Skip
an expensive step once a ceiling is passed:

```ts
export const frugal = step(polish, undefined, {
  when: (state) => (state.usage?.tokens ?? 0) < 100_000,
});
```

In a hand-written reducer, read `event.usage_total` and decide. See
[observability.md](./observability.md#usage-accounting).

## Retry a flaky call

Retries are part of the activity, not your handler:

```ts
export const summarise = activity("doc.summarise", {
  input: z.object({ text: z.string(), compact: z.boolean().optional() }),
  output: z.object({ summary: z.string() }),
  retry: { maxAttempts: 5, backoff: "exponential", initialMs: 2_000, maxMs: 60_000 },
  timeoutMs: 120_000,
});
```

Throw from the handler and the policy decides. If repeating the same request would fail
the same way, change the input on later attempts. Here `callModel` is your handler:

```ts
export const summariser = defineWorker({
  "doc.summarise": withRetryInput(callModel, (input, attempt) => ({ ...input, compact: attempt > 1 })),
});
```

See [activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#declaring-an-activity).

## Run a task for hours

Leave `timeoutMs` unset. A task is held by a lease that the SDK worker renews
automatically, so there is no duration ceiling. If the worker dies, the lease lapses and
the retry policy takes over. Pass `ctx.signal` to long calls so they stop when the lease
is lost. See [activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#leases-heartbeats-and-timeouts).

## Fan out, narrow or wide

For up to a few dozen items, fan out tasks inside the run:

```ts
export const narrow = fanOut(
  resize,
  (state) => resultOf(state, list).images.map((image) => ({ image })),
  { concurrency: 4 },
);
```

For hundreds or thousands, fan out child runs. One run with very many tasks slows down
sharply; child runs do not have that problem.

```ts
export const wide = fanOutRuns(
  "process-image",
  (state) => resultOf(state, list).images.map((image) => ({ image })),
  { concurrency: 20 },
);
```

Read results with `fanOutResultsOf` and `fanOutRunsResultsOf`. See
[workflows.md](./workflows.md#the-sequence-helper) and [limits.md](./limits.md#known-weak-spots).

## Tolerate a failure

```ts
step(notify, undefined, { onFailure: "continue" }),
fanOut(fetchSource, () => [{ url: "https://example.com" }], { concurrency: 4, onFailure: "continue" }),
```

A failed step stores `null` instead of failing the run, so narrow the value when you read
it.

## Stream progress to a UI

Durable progress is the journal. Follow it over SSE:

```ts
for await (const message of client.stream(runId)) {
  if (message.type === "journal") render(message.data.step_id, message.data.status);
  if (message.type === "emit") renderHint(message.data);
  if (message.type === "end") finish(message.data.status);
}
```

For extra detail that does not need to survive a reconnect, emit it from the reducer with
`cmd.emit("progress", { percent: 40 })`. Emits are not journaled. From a browser, use the
SSE form of `GET /v1/runs/{id}/events`; see [http-api.md](./http-api.md).

## Start a run idempotently

Choose the run id yourself. A second start with the same id does not create a second run.

```ts
await client.start("weekly-report", { team }, { runId: `weekly_${team}_${isoWeek}` });
```

`client.startFresh` joins a live run under that key, and starts a new one (`<id>_2`, `<id>_3`, …)
once the earlier runs have ended. See [http-api.md](./http-api.md).

## Sleep or wait until a time

```ts
export const reminder = sequence([step(sendInvite), sleep(3 * 86_400_000), step(sendReminder)]);
```

In a hand-written reducer use `cmd.timer({ ms })` or `cmd.timer({ atMs })` and handle
`on.timer`. A sleeping run holds no compute.

## Write a worker in another language

A worker is an HTTP endpoint. It verifies the signature, answers `202`, does the work and
calls back.

```python
import hashlib, hmac, json, requests

def handle_push(headers, raw_body: bytes):
    task_id, attempt, ts = headers["vlo-task-id"], headers["vlo-attempt"], headers["vlo-timestamp"]
    body_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw_body).hexdigest()
    expected = "v1=" + hmac.new(PUSH_SECRET, f"{task_id}.{attempt}.{ts}.{body_hash}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, headers["vlo-signature"]):
        return 401

    task = json.loads(raw_body)
    queue.submit(run_task, task)   # do the work after answering
    return 202

def run_task(task):
    output = predict(task["input"])
    requests.post(
        task["complete_url"] + "/complete",
        headers={"authorization": f"Bearer {VLO_TOKEN}"},
        json={"attempt": task["attempt"], "output": output, "usage": {"tokens": 1200}},
    )
```

Also reject a `vlo-timestamp` more than five minutes old, and heartbeat on
`{complete_url}/heartbeat` for work longer than the lease. The full protocol is in
[activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#push-mode-default-for-remote-queues).

## Pull tasks instead of receiving pushes

Set the queue to `mode: "pull"` and run a poller wherever the worker can reach the API:

```ts
await runPullWorker({ baseUrl: "https://vlo.example.com", token: process.env.VLO_TOKEN!, worker: mediaWorker });
```

See [activities-and-workers.md](./activities-and-workers.md#pull-mode).

## Compact a very long run

A run that loops for months should not carry its whole history. End it and start a
successor with fresh history:

```ts
return [state, [cmd.continueAsNew({ cursor: state.cursor })]];
```

The two runs are linked, and a parent is told once, by the run that finally closes. See
[workflows.md](./workflows.md#commands).

## Cancel a run

```ts
await client.cancel(runId);
```

The run ends as `cancelled`. Cancelling a run that has already ended does nothing.

---

---
url: /vlo/configuration.md
---
# Configuration

`vlo.config.ts` says where the code lives and how each environment is wired. It is a
TypeScript module the CLI imports; `defineConfig` gives you types and `env()` keeps secrets
out of the file.

```ts
import { defineConfig, env } from "@oona/vlo";

export default defineConfig({
  workflows: ["src/**/*.workflow.ts"],
  workers: ["src/**/*.worker.ts"],
  activities: ["src/**/activities.ts"],
  profiles: {
    local: { journal: "sqlite://.vlo/dev.db", blob: "file://.vlo/blobs" },
    prod: {
      journal: env("DATABASE_URL"),
      blob: "gcs://my-bucket/vlo",
      publicUrl: env("VLO_PUBLIC_URL"),
      roles: ["orchestrator", "api"],
      dispatcher: { mode: "loop", tickMs: 500 },
      queues: {
        llm: { url: env("VLO_QUEUE_LLM_URL"), secret: env("VLO_PUSH_SECRET") },
        media: { mode: "pull" },
      },
      auth: { token: env("VLO_TOKEN"), pushSecret: env("VLO_PUSH_SECRET") },
      port: 8080,
      deploy: { target: "cloud-run", region: "europe-west4" },
    },
  },
});
```

## File and loading rules

* Looked up as `vlo.config.ts`, `vlo.config.js`, then `vlo.config.mjs` in the working
  directory, or wherever `--config <path>` points.
* The module must `export default defineConfig({ … })`.
* It is imported by Node, not bundled: relative imports inside it (and inside the modules it
  points at) need explicit extensions, and path aliases are not resolved. A `.ts` config
  needs a Node that strips types natively; `.js` / `.mjs` always work.
* With no config file at all, the built-in default is used: workflows
  `**/*.workflow.{ts,js,mjs}`, workers `**/*.worker.{ts,js,mjs}`, one profile `local` with
  `sqlite://.vlo/dev.db` and `file://.vlo/blobs`, resolved against the working directory
  because there is no config file to be relative to.
* `defineConfig` throws when `profiles` is empty.

## Top level

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workflows` | `string \| string[]` | Globs, relative to the config file. Every match is imported. |
| `workers` | `string \| string[]` | Optional. Modules exporting `defineWorker(...)`. |
| `activities` | `string \| string[]` | Optional. Modules exporting `activity()` / `signal()` definitions to register. |
| `profiles` | `Record<string, Profile>` | At least one. |

Discovery is by export shape, not by file name: any export with `kind: "workflow"`,
`"worker"`, `"activity"` or `"signal"` from any matched module is collected, default or
named. Re-exporting an activity from a workflow file registers it. Named things are deduped
by `name`; `node_modules` is always excluded.

## `env(name, { optional? })`

Records the *name* of an environment variable. The value is resolved when the profile
loads; a missing required variable fails with a message naming it. `optional: true` yields
`undefined` instead. Any `Ref` field below accepts either a literal string or an `env()`.

`env()` returns an object, so it cannot be concatenated: write the full value into one
variable rather than `env("HOST") + "/path"`.

## `profiles.<name>`

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `journal` | `Ref` | required | `sqlite://<path>` (`sqlite://:memory:`, `sqlite://.vlo/x.db`, `sqlite:///abs/x.db`) or `postgres://…` / `postgresql://…`. A relative SQLite path resolves against the config file's directory. |
| `blob` | `Ref` | `file://.vlo/blobs` | `file://<dir>` or `gcs://<bucket>[/<prefix>]`. A relative `file://` directory resolves against the config file's directory. Payloads over 256 KiB go here. |
| `publicUrl` | `Ref` | none | Base URL peers reach this host on. Fills `complete_url` on pushes and the origin of signed links. `host` is a deprecated alias. |
| `port` | `number` | `4100` | Listening port. See precedence below. |
| `roles` | `Role[]` | all | `"orchestrator"`, `"api"`, `"worker:<queue>"`. Absent ⇒ orchestrator + api + a worker role for every queue an in-process worker declares. |
| `queues` | `Record<string, QueueProfile>` | `{}` | See below. |
| `auth` | `{ token?, pushSecret? }` | `{}` | Both `Ref`s. See below. |
| `dispatcher` | `DispatcherProfile` | `{ mode: "loop" }` | See below. |
| `deploy` | `DeployProfile` | none | Only read by `vlo deploy`. |

### `queues.<name>`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | Where the orchestrator pushes this queue's tasks (`https://…/v1/tasks/push`). Absent ⇒ in-process only. |
| `secret` | HMAC secret shared with the worker at `url`. Required for push; an empty secret refuses to push. |
| `mode` | `"push"` (default) or `"pull"`. Pull queues are never pushed; workers poll them. |

`vlo doctor` fails a queue that has neither a `url` nor an in-process worker.

### `auth`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `token` | Bearer token required on every control-plane route. Absent ⇒ open host. Also the default secret for signed links. |
| `pushSecret` | HMAC secret this host's `worker:*` roles verify inbound pushes with. |

`createHost` additionally accepts `callbackToken` (bearer a worker host sends on result
callbacks; defaults to `token`) and `linkSecret` (signed-link secret; falls back to `token`,
then `pushSecret`). Those two are not fields of the config profile.

### `dispatcher`

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `"loop"` | `"loop"` ticks on an interval and on every write. `"manual"` never ticks by itself: something must call `POST /v1/timers/tick` or `Host.drain()`. Use `manual` on serverless. |
| `tickMs` | `500` | Interval in loop mode. |

`createHost({ dispatcher })` also takes `batch` (50), `claimHoldMs` (30 000), `backoffBaseMs`
(1 000), `maxBackoffMs` (60 000), `unroutableBackoffMs` (60 000) and `workerId`.

### `deploy`

Never a secret: only names, regions and modes. Everything here is safe to write into a
generated file.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | required | `"cloud-run"` or `"vercel"`. |
| `project` | none | Cloud project id, printed into commands. |
| `region` | `"europe-west4"` | Cloud Run region. |
| `namePrefix` | `"vlo"` | Leading segment of every generated resource name: `<namePrefix>-<env>-<service>`. |
| `service` | `"vlo"` | Component segment of the per-env names. |
| `bucket` | from `blob` | Blob bucket; derived from a `gcs://` blob URL when absent. |
| `envs` | `["staging", "prod"]` | Environments the templates are instantiated for. |
| `secretName` | `"vlo"` | Middle segment of generated secret ids: `<namePrefix>-<env>-<secretName>-database-url` and friends. |
| `cron` | `"* * * * *"` | Schedule for the tick route on serverless targets. |

What each target renders is in [deployment.md](./deployment.md).

## Environment variables and precedence

| Variable | Read by | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VLO_PROFILE` | every verb | Profile to use when `--profile` is not given. `dev` also falls back to `local`, then to the only profile in the file. |
| `PORT` | `serve` | Listening port when `--port` is not given. Set by most container platforms. |
| `VLO_KERNEL_WASM` | host, `doctor` | Absolute path to a kernel wasm to load instead of the one shipped in the package. |
| anything named in `env()` | config load | Resolved into the profile. |

Precedence:

* Profile: `--profile` > `VLO_PROFILE` > (`dev` only) `local` > (`dev` only) the sole profile. Otherwise the error lists the profile names.
* Port: `--port` > `PORT` (`serve` only) > `profiles.<name>.port` > `4100`.
* Config path: `--config` > auto-detected file > built-in default.

## What the host receives

Loading a profile yields the options `serve()` / `createHost()` take: `journal`, `blob`,
`workflows`, `workers`, `activities`, `signals`, `queues`, `auth`, `roles`, `dispatcher`,
`publicUrl`, `port`. You can skip the config file entirely and call
`serve({ … })` from `@oona/vlo/host` yourself with the same fields plus `basePath`,
`streamPollMs`, `namespace`, `hostname` and `domains` (values from `defineDomain`, flattened
onto the four registries; `workflows` becomes optional when a domain supplies them).

url: /vlo/cli.md
---
# CLI

The `vlo` command ships with `@oona/vlo` (`npx vlo …`). Four verbs, one profile: whatever
runs on your laptop, what `doctor` checks and what `deploy` renders all come from the same
entry in `vlo.config.ts`. See [configuration.md](./configuration.md).

```
vlo dev    [--config <path>] [--profile <name>] [--port <n>]
vlo serve  --profile <name>  [--config <path>] [--port <n>]
vlo doctor --profile <name>  [--config <path>] [--json] [--no-migrate]
vlo deploy --profile <name>  [--config <path>] [--out deploy/vlo] [--apply]
vlo --help | -h
vlo --version
```

Shared flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--config <path>` | Config file to load instead of auto-detecting `vlo.config.{ts,js,mjs}`. |
| `--profile <name>` | Profile inside the config. Every verb falls back to `VLO_PROFILE`; `serve`, `doctor` and `deploy` fail without one, `dev` picks `local` or the only profile. |
| `--help`, `-h` | Print usage to stdout and exit 0. |
| `--version` | Print the SDK version to stdout and exit 0. |

`--help` and `--version` are being added alongside this documentation; earlier builds print
usage to stderr and exit 1 for any unknown verb.

## `vlo dev`

The whole engine on a laptop: SQLite journal, file blob store, every role in one process.

```
$ npx vlo dev
  ✓ journal  sqlite:///home/me/app/.vlo/dev.db
  ✓ found 2 workflows   example · hello
  ✓ found 1 worker   in-process
  ✓ api      http://localhost:4100
```

* Profile: `--profile`, else `VLO_PROFILE`, else `local`, else the only profile in the file;
  with no config file the built-in `local` profile is used.
* Relative `sqlite://` and `file://` paths resolve against the config file's directory, and
  the journal and blob store create their own directories.
* Migrates the journal, imports every module the globs match, binds the port, starts the
  dispatcher in the profile's mode (`loop` unless configured otherwise).
* No hot reload: restart after editing a workflow.
* The third line is one of `found N workers   in-process`, `workers   remote via queues …`,
  or a stderr warning `⚠ no workers found` when there are neither.
* Dispatcher warnings (a push refused, a task with no transport) go to stderr as `⚠ …`.
* `SIGINT` / `SIGTERM` stop the dispatcher, wait up to 5 s for in-process handlers, then
  close the journal.

## `vlo serve`

The production twin of `dev`: identical code path, no conveniences.

* `--profile` (or `VLO_PROFILE`) is required. There is no SQLite fallback.
* Nothing is created on disk.
* Port: `--port`, then `PORT`, then the profile's `port`, then `4100`.
* Prints the same ✓ lines as `dev`; `/healthz` answers `{ ok, roles, workflows }`.

`vlo serve --profile prod` is what the generated Cloud Run image runs.

## `vlo doctor`

Is this profile actually wired up? Every check is a real round trip, so it fails here
rather than three minutes into a deploy. Cheap enough to run on every boot of a new
environment.

```
$ vlo doctor --profile prod
  ✓ journal    postgres · commit round trip 4 ms
  ✓ migrate    schema up to date
  ✓ blob       gcs://my-bucket/vlo · 1 KiB round trip
  ✓ kernel     protocol 1 · 288 KiB
  ⚠ schemas    2/4 registered · missing example.plan · example.approve
               → these register on the next host boot
  ✓ queue:llm  push · https://workers.example.com/healthz reachable
  ✓ queue:media  pull · served by pollers
  ✓ roles      orchestrator · api · dispatcher loop
```

| Check | What it does | ⚠ / ✗ when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `journal` | Opens the URL and runs one empty write transaction (lock + commit). | ✗ unreachable, bad credentials, missing database, unsupported scheme. |
| `migrate` | Applies pending migrations. | ✗ migration failed; ⚠ skipped with `--no-migrate`. |
| `blob` | Writes a 1 KiB probe and reads it back. Content-addressed, so re-runs write nothing. | ✗ cannot write, digest mismatch, truncated read. |
| `kernel` | Finds the wasm, loads it, compares protocol versions. | ✗ not found or protocol mismatch; ⚠ over the 1 MiB budget. |
| `schemas` | Looks up every registered activity and signal hash in the `schemas` table. | ⚠ some not registered yet (a host boot registers them). |
| `queue:<name>` | One per queue. Push: `GET <url>/healthz` with a 3 s timeout. Pull: always ok. No URL: needs an in-process worker. | ✗ unreachable, unhealthy, no URL and no worker, URL not absolute; ⚠ push URL with no `secret`. |
| `roles` | Roles versus dispatcher mode. | ⚠ orchestrator in `manual` mode with no `deploy.cron`: nothing would ever tick. |

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--json` | Print the checks as a JSON array instead of the table. |
| `--no-migrate` | Never write to the journal. A missing schema then shows up as a failed commit. |

`--json` shape, one object per check:

```json
[
  { "check": "journal", "status": "ok", "detail": "sqlite · commit round trip 1 ms" },
  { "check": "schemas", "status": "warn", "detail": "1/2 registered · missing demo.echo",
    "hint": "these register on the next host boot" }
]
```

`status` is `"ok"`, `"warn"` or `"fail"`; `hint` is present on anything that is not ok.
Any `fail` sets exit code 1, so a pipeline can gate on it.

## `vlo deploy`

Renders the platform files for a profile and stops there. Generation is not application:
nothing touches a cloud account without a human running the printed commands.

```
$ vlo deploy --profile prod
  ✓ deploy/vlo/cloud-run/Dockerfile
  ✓ deploy/vlo/cloud-run/cloudbuild.yaml
  ✓ deploy/vlo/cloud-run/cloud-run-vlo.tf
  ✓ deploy/vlo/cloud-run/cloudbuild-vlo.tf
  ✓ deploy/vlo/cloud-run/README.md
```

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--out <dir>` | Output directory, relative to the working directory. Default `deploy/vlo`. |
| `--apply` | After writing, print the exact `gcloud` / `terraform` / `vercel` commands to run. Nothing is executed. |

Requires `deploy: { target: "cloud-run" | "vercel", … }` on the profile; the error names
the profile otherwise. Resolved secrets (the journal URL, tokens) never reach a generated
file; templates read them from environment variables or Secret Manager at run time. The
file-by-file contents are described in [deployment.md](./deployment.md).

## Exit codes

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The verb finished; `doctor` found no ✗. |
| `1` | Unknown verb (usage on stderr); any thrown error (message on stderr), including a missing `--profile`, an unknown profile, an unset `env()` variable; `doctor` with at least one ✗. |

## Running from source

From a checkout of the repository:

```sh
pnpm --filter @oona/vlo exec tsx src/cli.ts dev --config ../../../examples/hello/vlo.config.ts
```

The kernel wasm is committed at `sdk/ts/sdk/wasm/vlo_kernel_bg.wasm`; rebuild it after
kernel changes with `./scripts/build-kernel.sh` (needs `wasm-pack` and the pinned Rust
toolchain), or point `VLO_KERNEL_WASM` at a freshly built file. `pnpm --filter @oona/vlo
test` runs the SDK suite on SQLite; set `VLO_TEST_DATABASE_URL` to also run it on Postgres.

Every verb is also a library call: `dev()`, `serveCommand()`, `doctor()` / `runChecks()`
and `deploy()` under `sdk/ts/sdk/src/cli/` take an options object and return what they
started, checked or wrote.
