# Architecture

Five layers, three sequences, three roles. Source: `src/host/**`, `crates/**`.

## Layers

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph APP["Your app"]
    ACT["activities · Zod schemas"]
    WF["workflows · pure reducers"]
    WK["workers · any language"]
    AG["@oona/vlo/agent · decision · agentLoop"]
    CL["Client · createClient or HTTP"]
  end
  subgraph K["Kernel · Rust on wasm · no I/O"]
    ENV["envelope validation · step state machine"]
    RD["prepare_event · reduce_step · write-set"]
    RT["state hash · retry planning · id derivation"]
  end
  subgraph H["Host · @oona/vlo/host on Node"]
    TR["applyEvent · one transaction per event"]
    DI["Dispatcher · outbox stages"]
    RO["Router · /v1 routes · SSE"]
  end
  subgraph AD["Adapters"]
    J["Journal"]
    B["BlobStore"]
    T["TaskTransport"]
  end
  subgraph INF["Your infrastructure"]
    PG[("Postgres")]
    SQ[("SQLite file")]
    FS[("directory or bucket")]
    HTTP["worker HTTP endpoint"]
  end
  ACT --> WF
  ACT --> WK
  AG --> WF
  CL --> RO
  WF --> TR
  TR --> K
  K --> TR
  TR --> J
  TR --> B
  DI --> J
  DI --> T
  RO --> TR
  RO --> DI
  J --> PG
  J --> SQ
  B --> FS
  T --> HTTP
  T --> WK
  HTTP --> WK
```

The kernel is closed: the five event kinds, seven statuses and seven commands cannot be
extended by a project. Everything above it is your code; everything below it is an adapter
with a small interface (`Journal`, `BlobStore`, `TaskTransport`).

## The write path

Every durable change goes through `applyEvent` (`src/host/transition.ts`): one transaction,
one event, one write-set.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Source
  participant H as Host applyEvent
  participant J as Journal
  participant K as Kernel
  participant R as Reducer
  participant O as Outbox
  S->>H: EventInput
  H->>J: BEGIN · lockRun
  H->>J: getState (checkpoint)
  H->>K: stateHash(checkpoint) matches stored hash?
  H->>K: prepareEvent
  alt mode reduce
    H->>R: reduce(state, reducerEvent)
    R-->>H: state' + commands
    H->>K: reduceStep
  end
  K-->>H: Transition (write-set)
  H->>J: applyTransition · events · run_state · tasks · timers · waits · child rows
  H->>J: COMMIT
  H-->>S: outcome
  H->>O: emit side channel · task_scheduled · kick
  Note over O: next dispatcher pass pushes the tasks
```

Details that matter:

* The checkpoint is verified before folding. A missing checkpoint or a `bundle_digest` that
  differs from the run's pin is rebuilt from `seq 0` inside the same transaction.
* A reducer throw rolls the transaction back; the host then appends a `fail` marker whose
  payload is the event that was being folded, and the run is `failed`.
* A kernel refusal with code `unknown_step`, `already_terminal` or `bad_seq` is treated as a
  redelivery and answers `duplicate`; other refusals surface as `IllegalEvent`.
* Signals that were buffered before a wait existed are delivered as follow-up events right
  after commit.
* Cross-run effects never happen inside the fold. A `spawn` writes a `created` row; the
  outbox starts it in its own transaction. A closed child is noticed by the outbox and folded
  into the parent as a `child` event.

## The dispatcher

`Dispatcher` (`src/host/dispatcher.ts`) is the only thing that turns rows into effects. One
pass runs six idempotent stages, each claiming rows for `claimHoldMs` so several orchestrators
never do the same work:

| Stage | Claims | Produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| start runs | `runs.status = 'created'` | the `started` event |
| push tasks | `tasks` scheduled and undispatched, not on a pull queue | a push to the queue's transport, then `task/running` + lease |
| fire timers | `timers` due and unfired | `timer/succeeded`; the fired flag and the event commit together |
| reap leases | `tasks` running with `lease_until_ms` in the past | `task/failed` or `task/retrying` with `cause: heartbeat_lost` |
| reap timeouts | `tasks` running past `dispatched_at_ms + timeout_ms` | the same with `cause: timeout` |
| notify parents | closed child runs not yet notified | a `child` event on the parent; a `continued` child is marked notified without one, because its successor carries the parent link |

In `loop` mode a pass runs every `tickMs` and on every `kick()` after a commit. In `manual`
mode nothing runs until `host.tick()`, `host.drain()` or `POST /v1/timers/tick`.

## The task lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant H as Host
  participant J as Journal
  participant W as Worker
  C->>H: POST /v1/runs
  H->>J: runs row status created
  H->>J: seq 1 started → reduce → seq 2 task scheduled + tasks row (one txn)
  H->>W: POST queue url · PushedTask · vlo-signature
  W-->>H: 202 accepted
  H->>J: seq 3 task running · lease_until · worker_id
  loop while the handler runs
    W->>H: POST /v1/tasks/{id}/heartbeat {attempt}
    H->>J: extend lease_until
  end
  W->>H: POST /v1/tasks/{id}/complete {attempt, output, usage}
  H->>H: validate output against the activity schema
  H->>J: seq 4 task succeeded → reduce → next task or complete (one txn)
  H-->>C: GET /v1/runs/{id}/events · SSE
```

Statuses a task step moves through: `scheduled` → `running` → `succeeded` | `failed` |
`retrying` (→ `scheduled` again on the next attempt) | `cancelled`. Execution is
at-least-once, recording exactly-once: the first terminal result for an attempt wins, a later
one answers `duplicate`. A worker that dies stops heartbeating; the lease reaper fails the
attempt with `heartbeat_lost` and the retry policy decides whether a fresh attempt (new
idempotency key, back in the outbox) or a final failure follows. A pull worker
(`POST /v1/tasks/poll`) enters the same sequence at the "202 accepted" point: the host records
`running` and the lease before handing the task out.

## Roles and processes

A process holds a subset of three roles; `createHost({ roles })` defaults to all of them plus
`worker:<queue>` for every in-process worker.

| Role | Owns | Routes it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orchestrator` | the dispatcher, `tick`, `drain` | `POST /v1/timers/tick` |
| `api` | the control plane | `/v1/runs/**`, `/v1/tasks/poll`, `/v1/tasks/{id}/*` |
| `worker:<queue>` | handlers for that queue, in-process and over inbound push | `POST /v1/tasks/push` |

Typical splits:

* **Laptop, CI, small self-host**: one process, every role, SQLite, file blobs.
* **Long-lived service plus workers**: `orchestrator` + `api` on one service; `worker:media`
  in containers that either receive pushes at a queue URL or run `runPullWorker`.
* **Serverless**: `orchestrator` + `api` + in-process workers in a route handler with
  `dispatcher: { mode: "manual" }`, a cron on the tick route, and `basePath` set to the mount
  point. Push queues can point at other functions.

Any process with `api` may accept a request for any run; only a process holding the
run's journal lock appends to it, one transaction at a time. Several `orchestrator` processes
may share a Postgres journal; a SQLite journal wants one.

---

---
url: /vlo/kernel-protocol.md
---
# Kernel protocol

The kernel is a Rust library (`crates/kernel`) with no I/O, no clock and no randomness of its
own, compiled to wasm (`crates/kernel-wasm`) and loaded in Node by `src/kernel/load.ts`.
Every export is a JSON string in and a JSON string out. This page is the contract between the
host and that boundary. Types: `crates/types`, mirrored by hand in `src/kernel/protocol.ts`.

## Exports and versioning

`PROTOCOL_VERSION` is `1` on both sides; `loadKernel()` refuses a wasm whose
`kernel_version().protocol` differs. `kernel_version` also reports the crate version and a
`features` list (`canonical_json_v1`, `state_hash_v1`, `refold_v1`), which is additive only.

| wasm export | `Kernel` method | Input → output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kernel_version` | `version()` | `{ version, protocol, features }` |
| `validate_event` | `validateEvent(event)` | `EventInput` → `{ normalized: EventInput }` |
| `prepare_event` | `prepareEvent({ run, kernel_state?, state?, event })` | `Prepared` (see below) |
| `reduce_step` | `reduceStep({ run, kernel_state, event, reduction })` | `Transition` |
| `compute_state_hash` | `stateHash({ kernel_state, state })` | `{ hash }` |
| `plan_retry` | `planRetry({ policy, attempt, cause, random })` | `RetryPlan` |
| `refold_check` | `refoldCheck({ expected, actual })` | `RefoldCheckOutput` |
| `derive_ids` | `deriveIds({ run_id, step_id, attempt })` | `{ task_id, idempotency_key, child_run_id }` |

Every export returns `KernelResult<T>`: `{"ok":true,"value":…}` or
`{"ok":false,"error":{"code","message","seq"?,"step_id"?}}`. The kernel never panics
(`panic = "abort"` in the wasm profile makes that a hard requirement); the twelve codes are
listed in [errors](errors.md).

## Envelope

An `EventInput` is what the host submits; an `Envelope` is the journaled form, which adds
`seq`, `state_hash`, and the run's `parent_run_id` / `parent_step_id`.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `task`, `timer`, `signal`, `child`, `marker` |
| `status` | `scheduled`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `retrying`, `cancelled`, `awaiting_signal` |
| `cause` | `timeout`, `heartbeat_lost`, `app_error`, `user_cancel`, `schema_violation`, `nondeterminism_detected` |
| `usage` | `{ cpu_ms, tokens, cost_micro_usd }`, integers |
| `ts_ms`, `random` | The host's clock and 32 hex chars of entropy, journaled so a replay sees the same values |
| `payload` / `payload_ref` | Byte-exact JSON text, or a `blob://sha256/…` ref; at most one of the two |
| `schema_ref`, `error` | Optional; never interpreted by the kernel |

The kernel routes on the header alone (`classify.rs`). Markers are keyed by `step_id`:
`start` (status `succeeded`), `cancel`, `fail` (status `failed`), `nondeterminism`
(cause `nondeterminism_detected`); the kernel itself writes `complete` and `continue`.

The step state machine allows these edges (`step_machine.rs`); anything else is
`illegal_transition`:

```
scheduled → running | succeeded | failed | retrying | cancelled
running   → succeeded | failed | retrying | cancelled | awaiting_signal
retrying  → scheduled | succeeded | failed | cancelled
awaiting_signal → running | succeeded | cancelled
```

Terminal steps are pruned from `kernel_state.steps` (`closed_steps` counts them), so a late
event for one is `unknown_step`.

## Two-phase fold

`prepare_event` classifies the event and answers one of two modes:

* `{ "mode": "reduce", "reducer_event", "init_input"?, "kernel_state" }` — call the reducer
  with `reducer_event` (and `init(init_input)` first for `started`), then pass the result to
  `reduce_step`.
* `{ "mode": "lifecycle", "transition" }` — pure bookkeeping (task `running`, `retrying`,
  `cancelled`; run `cancel`, `fail`, `nondeterminism`). Apply the transition as-is; the user
  state is echoed from the checkpoint and re-hashed with the new kernel state.

The five reducer events, each carrying `ts_ms`, `random` and `usage_total`:

| `type` | Extra fields |
| --- | --- |
| `started` | `input` |
| `task_done` | `step_id`, `attempt`, `activity`, `status` (`succeeded` or `failed`), `output?`, `cause?`, `error?`, `usage` |
| `signal` | `step_id`, `name`, `payload` |
| `timer` | `step_id` |
| `child_done` | `step_id`, `child_run_id`, `status`, `output?` |

The seven commands a reducer may return (`Reduction = { state: string, commands }`):

| `type` | Fields | Opens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `task` | `activity`, `input`, `schema_ref?`, `queue?` (default `default`), `retry?`, `lease_ttl_ms?` (default 60 000), `timeout_ms?`, `id?` | a task step, attempt 1 |
| `timer` | `fire_in_ms?` or `fire_at_ms?`, `id?` | a timer step |
| `spawn` | `workflow`, `input`, `id?` | a child step with a derived `child_run_id` |
| `await_signal` | `name`, `schema_ref?`, `timeout_ms?`, `id?` | a signal step in `awaiting_signal`; with `timeout_ms`, also a timer step `<id>:timeout` and its `NewTimer`. Whichever fires first, the kernel prunes the other, so the reducer sees one event and a late event on the loser is `unknown_step`. |
| `emit` | `channel`, `data` | nothing durable |
| `complete` | `output` | the `complete` marker; run → `completed` |
| `continue_as_new` | `input` | the `continue` marker; run → `continued` |

Default step ids are `<kind>#<n>` from the monotonic `step_no` (`task#1`, `timer#2`,
`child#3`, `signal#4`); an explicit `id` must be unique among open steps. At most one
completion per reduction and nothing after it.

## The write-set

`reduce_step` validates every command and returns a declarative `Transition`. The journal
applies it atomically under the run lock and never interprets commands.

| Field | Type | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run` | `RunPatch` | `{ status, last_seq }` for the `runs` row. Status is derived from the step map: `awaiting_signal` when only signal steps and their `<id>:timeout` deadline timers are open, else `running`, or the completion's status. |
| `kernel_state` | `KernelState` | `{ v, status, step_no, steps, closed_steps, usage_total }` |
| `state`, `state_hash`, `state_inline` | | The reducer's state (byte-exact), its hash, and whether it fits inline |
| `events` | `Envelope[]` | The trigger first, then one lifecycle `scheduled` / `awaiting_signal` event per opened step and one marker for a completion. All carry the same `state_hash`. |
| `tasks` | `NewTask[]` | `task_id`, `step_id`, `attempt`, `activity`, `queue`, `schema_ref?`, `input`, `idempotency_key`, `retry`, `lease_ttl_ms`, `timeout_ms?` |
| `task_updates` | `TaskUpdate[]` | `{ task_id, attempt, status, not_before_ms? }` — the trigger's own row is settled here, cancels on run close, `scheduled` after a retry |
| `timers` | `NewTimer[]` | `{ step_id, fire_at_ms }` |
| `spawns` | `NewSpawn[]` | `{ step_id, child_run_id, workflow, input }`; the host turns these into `created` run rows |
| `signal_waits` | `SignalWait[]` | `{ step_id, name, schema_ref?, expires_at_ms? }`; `expires_at_ms` is informational, the deadline itself is the paired timer |
| `emits` | `Emit[]` | `{ channel, data }`; the host publishes them after commit |
| `completion?` | `Completion` | `{ status, output? }` |
| `continue_as_new?` | `ContinueAsNew` | `{ input }`; the host turns it into a `created` successor row whose id is `derive_ids(run_id, "continue").child_run_id` |

## Retry planning

`plan_retry({ policy, attempt, cause, random })` is pure: the only entropy is the journaled
`random`. `RetryPolicy` is `{ max_attempts, backoff: "fixed" | "exponential", initial_ms,
max_ms, factor, jitter: "none" | "full" }`. The plan is `{ retry: false }` when the cause is
`schema_violation`, `user_cancel` or `nondeterminism_detected`, or when `attempt >=
max_attempts` (`max_attempts: 1` never retries). Otherwise
`{ retry: true, next_attempt: attempt + 1, delay_ms }` where the base delay is
`initial_ms` (fixed) or `min(initial_ms × factor^(attempt−1), max_ms)` (exponential), and full
jitter scales it by the first 16 hex chars of `random` over `2^64 − 1`. A fixture:
attempt 2, exponential from 1000 ms with the fixture's `random` plans `delay_ms: 1246`.

## Hashing rules

* **Canonical JSON**: parse, then re-serialise compact with object keys sorted. Whitespace
  and key order never matter; `{"a":1,"b":2}` and `{ "b": 2, "a": 1 }` hash alike.
* **No floats in hashed inputs**: `Usage`, `RetryPolicy` and `KernelState` are integers only.
* **Byte-exact JSON as strings**: the user state, payloads and inputs cross the boundary as
  strings and are stored as `text`, so the bytes the kernel saw are the bytes it hashes again.
* `state_hash = sha256("vlo1" ‖ 0x00 ‖ canon(kernel_state) ‖ 0x00 ‖ canon(state))`, hex. The
  `vlo1` prefix is a domain separator.
* `refold_check` compares two `{ seq, hash }[]` lists and reports the first divergent seq
  with both hashes, or `{ matches: true }`. The host's rebuild path
  (`rebuildCheckpoint`) does the same comparison per event as it folds, so it stops at the
  first divergence rather than folding past it.

## Schema hash

Activity and signal versions are content hashes computed by the SDK, not the kernel; the
kernel only carries `schema_ref` through. They are still a protocol, because any SDK must
mint the same `schema_ref` for the same definition.

* **Projection.** Before hashing, every schema object at every depth drops the annotation
  keywords `$schema`, `$id`, `$comment`, `title`, `description`, `examples`, `default`,
  `deprecated`, `readOnly`, `writeOnly`. The entries of `properties`, `patternProperties`,
  `dependentSchemas`, `$defs` and `definitions` are name-keyed: names are kept verbatim
  (a property may be called `default`) and only their values are projected. Arrays keep
  their order. Nothing else is rewritten: two emitters that disagree on validation
  semantics (say `anyOf` with `null` versus `type: [..., "null"]`) produce different hashes
  by design.
* **Envelope.** Activities hash
  `{ "v": 1, "name", "input": <projected>, "output": <projected>, "retry": <RetryPolicy> }`;
  signals hash `{ "v": 1, "name", "schema": <projected> }`. `retry` is the resolved wire
  policy (`max_attempts`, `backoff`, `initial_ms`, `max_ms`, `factor`, `jitter`).
* **Encoding.** Canonical JSON as above (sorted keys, compact, no floats), SHA-256, first
  16 lowercase hex characters. `schema_ref = "<name>@<hash>"`.
* **Versioning.** `v` is `SCHEMA_HASH_VERSION`. A change to the projection or the envelope
  bumps it, so the move is explicit; the rule is never changed under the same `v`.
* **Fixtures.** `fixtures/schema-hash/*.json` are golden cases: each lists `cases` (schemas
  as an emitter would produce them) that must all project to `projected` and hash to
  `hash`. `test/schema-hash.test.ts` replays them; a second-language SDK runs the same
  files.

## ID derivation

`task_id = "<run_id>:<step_id>"`, `idempotency_key = "<run_id>:<step_id>:<attempt>"`,
`child_run_id = "run_" + sha256(task_id)[0..26]`. All are pure functions of
`(run_id, step_id, attempt)`, so a re-push or a rebuilt checkpoint names the same task.

## Schema, fixtures, build

* `schema/kernel-protocol.schema.json` is generated from `crates/types` with `schemars`.
  `cargo test -p vlo-types` fails on drift; `UPDATE_SCHEMA=1 cargo test -p vlo-types`
  rewrites it.
* `fixtures/kernel/*.json` are golden `{ export, input, output }` cases (43 today) produced by
  the native tests through the same `api` module the wasm wraps.
  `UPDATE_FIXTURES=1 cargo test -p vlo-kernel` regenerates them. `src/kernel/kernel.test.ts`
  replays every fixture through the compiled wasm, so a mismatch means the committed wasm
  drifted from the Rust source.
  One field is masked in both replays: `kernel_version.json` holds `"<crate version>"` in
  place of the version, because a release bumps the crate while the committed wasm keeps
  the version it was built at. Both harnesses still check that the real value is a semver.
* `scripts/build-kernel.sh` runs `wasm-pack build --release --target web` on
  `crates/kernel-wasm`, remaps source paths so the artifact is reproducible on one platform,
  writes `sdk/ts/sdk/wasm/`, and fails over 1 MiB. The output is committed; a JS consumer
  never needs a Rust toolchain.
* `VLO_KERNEL_WASM=/path/to/vlo_kernel_bg.wasm` makes the loader (and `vlo doctor`) use
  another artifact. CI builds fresh, then runs the fixture replay against both the committed
  and the fresh wasm; byte drift between platforms is reported, not fatal.

Minimal use of the interface, lifted from the tests:

```ts
const kernel = await loadKernel();
const prepared = kernel.prepareEvent({ run, event });
if (prepared.ok && prepared.value.mode === "reduce") {
  const reduced = kernel.reduceStep({
    run, kernel_state: prepared.value.kernel_state, event,
    reduction: { state: JSON.stringify({ phase: "work" }),
                 commands: [{ type: "task", activity: "plan", input: { a: 1 } }] },
  });
  // reduced.value.tasks[0].idempotency_key === "run_ts:task#1:1"
}
```

---
# Design decisions

The choices that shape the engine, each as decision, reason and what it costs. Nothing here is
a roadmap; it is why the code looks the way it does.

## A reducer kernel instead of replayed linear code

**Decision.** A workflow is `(state, event) → (state, commands)`. State is the snapshot; the
kernel folds one event per transition and never runs workflow code otherwise.

**Why.** Linear `await` code has to be re-executed from the top to resume, which needs a
frozen realm or sandbox for determinism, a poll or asyncify contract to suspend, and replay
cost proportional to history. A reducer never suspends: there is no stack to save, no realm
to freeze, and recovery is "load the checkpoint, verify its hash, continue".

**Consequence.** Pipelines are written as phases (`sequence`, `fanOut`, `waitFor`, `sleep`)
or as hand-written handlers, not as `await a(); await b();`. A linear layer could be built
later on top of the same journal; it would not change the kernel.

## The journal is the queue; brokers only as a transport

**Decision.** The `tasks` table is the outbox and the lease. There is no message broker in
the write path. `TaskTransport` (HTTP push today, in-process for a local worker) is delivery
only; the row is the only source of truth.

**Why.** A broker gives you a second source of truth, an ack deadline that caps task
duration, and one more service on the hot path. A row committed in the same transaction as
the event gives exactly-once recording, lease-and-heartbeat with no duration ceiling,
completion from anywhere at any time, and a crash between "persisted" and "pushed" that
loses nothing.

**Consequence.** Fan-out throughput is bounded by the database (low thousands of tasks per
second on Postgres). Teams with an existing broker can add a transport adapter that carries
the pushed task; the journal still records it.

## Rust kernel on wasm, with a size budget and a semantic gate

**Decision.** The kernel is Rust with zero I/O, compiled to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` via
`wasm-bindgen`, committed under `sdk/ts/sdk/wasm/`, capped at 1 MiB. CI rebuilds it and
requires both the committed and the fresh artifact to pass every golden fixture.

**Why.** One implementation of the envelope rules, hashing and retry maths serves Node now
and any other host later, and a pure library is the easiest thing to test exhaustively
(proptests, an exhaustive step-edge table, fixtures). Byte-identical wasm across macOS and
Linux toolchains is not achievable in practice, so the gate is on behaviour instead.

**Consequence.** JS consumers never need a Rust toolchain. Kernel changes require rebuilding
and committing the wasm and regenerating fixtures; `VLO_KERNEL_WASM` lets you test another
build in place.

## A write-set kernel: the kernel returns rows, the host writes them

**Decision.** `reduce_step` returns a declarative `Transition` — events, checkpoint, new
tasks, task updates, timers, spawns, signal waits, emits, completion — and the journal applies
it atomically without interpreting commands.

**Why.** A kernel that owns the database cannot compile to wasm and would force a native host.
Splitting "decide" from "persist" keeps the kernel pure and testable, and makes every journal
adapter a dumb applier of the same shape.

**Consequence.** Journal adapters are small (one SQL text for both dialects) and can be
conformance-tested with `journalConformance`. Cross-run effects (starting a child, notifying a
parent) happen in later transactions through the outbox, never inside the fold.

## Hashed JSON is kept as text

**Decision.** `state`, `kernel_state`, `payload`, `input` and `output` are `text` columns.
Only `search`, `usage` and `retry_policy` are `jsonb` on Postgres.

**Why.** `jsonb` normalises key order and numeric lexemes. The re-fold check compares the
hash of what the kernel wrote with the hash of what it reads back; any rewrite in between is a
false nondeterminism.

**Consequence.** You cannot index into state with `jsonb` operators. Put queryable attributes
in `search` when starting a run.

## File and GCS blobs, with a 256 KiB offload

**Decision.** Anything larger than 256 KiB leaves the journal for a content-addressed blob
store; `file://` and `gcs://` are built in. References are `blob://sha256/<hex>`.

**Why.** History rows should stay small enough that folding thousands of events is cheap, and
a content address makes retries and duplicates free. GCS with Application Default
Credentials matches the first production target; a directory matches a laptop and CI.

**Consequence.** Every oversized payload costs a blob round trip on the write path. Other
stores (S3, Vercel Blob) are adapters to add; the interface is two methods.

## Push by default, signed with an HMAC

**Decision.** The dispatcher POSTs the full task to the queue's URL and expects `202`; the
worker completes later through `complete_url`. Every push carries
`vlo-signature: v1=hmac-sha256(secret, task_id.attempt.ts.sha256(body))` and is refused
outside a five-minute window. Pull (`mode: "pull"`) and in-process are the alternatives.

**Why.** Push lets workers scale to zero and live in serverless functions, and a signature
bound to task, attempt and time means a queue URL alone cannot be fed forged or replayed
tasks. Pull exists for workers behind a NAT or on hardware the orchestrator cannot reach.

**Consequence.** Every push queue needs a shared `secret`; the dispatcher refuses to push
unsigned. Workers must be idempotent on `idempotency_key`: delivery is at-least-once.

## A manual dispatcher plus a cron for serverless

**Decision.** `dispatcher: { mode: "manual" }` never arms an interval and ignores `kick()`.
Progress comes from `host.drain({ maxMs })`, called by the request that started or signalled
a run, and from a cron hitting `POST /v1/timers/tick?drain=1`.

**Why.** A serverless platform may freeze the process the moment a response is sent. An
unattended background tick would leave tasks marked `running` with nobody behind them; an
awaited, time-boxed drain finishes what it started, and the cron catches whatever a crashed
invocation left in the outbox.

**Consequence.** A run's chain of in-process steps advances within one invocation; anything
that parks (a timer, a remote worker, a signal) waits at most one cron interval. `vlo doctor`
warns when a manual orchestrator has no `deploy.cron`.

## Budget is a reducer decision

**Decision.** The kernel banks every attempt's `usage` into `usage_total` and hands it to the
reducer on every event. Budget enforcement lives in `@oona/vlo/agent`, which parks an exhausted
run on a top-up signal instead of failing it.

**Why.** An engine-level interceptor would need policy the kernel cannot know (what a token
costs, what a ceiling means, whether to park or fail). Trustworthy accounting is the only part
that must be engine-level, because a reducer cannot see a failed attempt's spend any other
way.

**Consequence.** Any workflow, not just an agent, can read `usage_total` and decide. There is
no price table: `cost_micro_usd` is whatever the worker reports.

## One checkpoint, verified by hash, rebuilt from zero

**Decision.** `run_state` holds exactly one checkpoint per run, rewritten in the same
transaction as every event. On load the host re-hashes it; a mismatch, a missing row or a
different bundle digest triggers a full fold from `seq 0`, comparing each transition's hash
with the journaled one.

**Why.** Folding is calling a pure function once per input event, which is milliseconds for
thousands of events, so a "last N events" window buys nothing. A per-event hash pinpoints
the exact seq where a reducer stopped agreeing with its own history.

**Consequence.** A run failed with `nondeterminism_detected` is a bug in the reducer, never
retried. Long-lived runs compact history with `continue_as_new`.

# TypeScript API

The reference for every symbol `@oona/vlo` exports, generated from the source. The package
has four entry points; import from the one that matches what you are writing.

| Entry point | Import it when |
| --- | --- |
| [`@oona/vlo`](/api/index/) | You are writing workflows, activities and signals. The authoring surface: nothing here touches I/O. |
| [`@oona/vlo/host`](/api/host/) | You are running Vlo: the host, journals, blob stores, transports, the client and the errors they raise. |
| [`@oona/vlo/agent`](/api/agent/) | You are building a decide → act → evaluate loop with a budget. |
| [`@oona/vlo/testing`](/api/testing/) | You are testing your own journal implementation, or need a fake clock. |
